Abstract:
Over recent years, ultrasonic atomization, especially with regard to liquid metals, has become an object of increased interest, mainly from industry, for additive manufacturing, but also from investigators, for research purposes. A strong correlation between the average particle size, distribution of particle sizes, and other process parameters like frequency and vibration amplitude was noted based on the analysis of available theoretical studies, simulations and experiments. The influence of parameters of the atomized fluid-like viscosity and surface tension on process parameters was also mentioned. The objective of this study is further research on the feasibility of using ultrasonic atomization to examine the properties of liquids, especially metals in liquid state. It attempts to close a gap in existing knowledge in searching for a new, possibly simple and cost-effective method to study the properties of liquid metals and further clarify the relationship between ultrasonic atomization parameters (amplitude, frequency, characteristics of metal being spilled on a vibrating surface) and obtained atomization results meant by average particle size and atomization time. Using numerical modeling (finite element method and computational fluid dynamics) as a methodology, combined with tests of using ultrasonic atomization as an instrument to determine properties of liquid metals, was considered as an introduction to a series of experiments. These tests were followed by real experiments that are also presented. At the first stage, numerical modeling was applied to a case of a specific liquid being spilled over a vibrating surface of different angles of inclination and specified, constant frequency and amplitude. The results of the simulation are in line with the current state of knowledge about ultrasonic atomization. Moreover, they can provide some more information on scalability, thus easing the comparison of the results of other experiments presented in the available literature. As a result, the relationship between fluid properties and the average size of atomized particles was demonstrated independently of the surface inclination angle. In the same way, the dependence of successful atomization on a sufficiently thin layer of a liquid was demonstrated. Thirdly, a correlation between the aforementioned layer thickness and the value of vibration amplitude has also been shown. Taking all the above into consideration, ultrasonic atomization can also be considered a research method and can be applied to study the properties of liquid metals. Further research, simulations and experimentation will be conducted to verify, develop and describe this method in full.

Abstract:
The significant growth of Additive Manufacturing (AM), visible over the last ten years, has driven an increase in demand for small gradation metallic powders of a size lower than 100 µm. Until now, most affordable powders for AM have been produced using gas atomization. Recently, a new, alternative method of powder production based on ultrasonic atomization with melting by electric arc has appeared. This paper summarizes the preliminary research results of AM samples made of two AISI 316L steel powder batches, one of which was obtained during Ultrasonic Atomization (UA) and the other during Plasma Arc Gas Atomization (PAGA). The comparison starts from powder particle statistical distribution, chemical composition analysis, density, and flowability measurements. After powder analysis, test samples were produced using AM to observe the differences in microstructure, porosity, and hardness. Finally, the test campaign covered an analysis of mechanical properties, including tensile testing with Digital Image Correlation (DIC) and Charpy’s impact tests. A comparative study of parts made of ultrasonic and gas atomization powders confirms the likelihood that both methods can deliver material of similar properties.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Copper is a critical material for energy transition and green technologies, making its sustainable use increasingly important. Its superior thermal and electrical conductivity make it highly well-suited for additive manufacturing (AM). In this study, copper sourced from offshore electrical cables was upcycled to produce high-quality metal powder for AM. The scrap was processed to separate the metal from plastic and rubber, then refined through ultrasonic atomization, achieving a purity of ~99.5% wt.% with minimal impurities. Characterization demonstrated good flowability, apparent and tap densities, and a well-distributed particle size. To assess its performance in AM, the powder was printed using Directed Energy Deposition (DED) with a laser beam, confirming its high printability and compatibility with the base material. Finally, a comparative Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) revealed a significant environmental advantage of the recycling-based process over conventional mining, reducing global warming potential by more than 70%. These findings highlight the importance of feedstock origin in AM sustainability and support the adoption of circular economy strategies to lower the environmental footprint of advanced manufacturing.</jats:p>

                                   3.4. Oxygen and Nitrogen Contents After Recycling Atomization

                           The oxygen and nitrogen contents measured in the initial gas-atomized powder
                       and in powders obtained by ultrasonic atomization are presented in Figure 8. The re-
                           cycled powders exhibit a consistently higher oxygen concentration compared to the
                             reference material, whereas the nitrogen content remains nearly unchanged within
                           experimental scatter.





                             Figure 8. Oxygen and nitrogen contents in the initial gas-atomized powder and in ultrasonically
                            atomized powders produced under different processing conditions.

                           The analysis was performed by inert gas fusion, which determines the total oxygen
                           content irrespective of whether oxygen is present in dissolved form or bound in oxide
                            phases. Therefore, the observed increase reflects a real change in the oxygen balance of
                            the material. The absence of a corresponding rise in nitrogen indicates that additional
                        oxygen was not introduced during handling in air (e.g., moisture adsorption or surface
                          contamination at ambient temperature), since such exposure would typically affect both
                              gases. Instead, the change is associated with processes occurring at elevated temperatures.
                           The most probable origin of the increased oxygen content is additional oxidation
                          during high-temperature stages of the processing route, i.e., during PBF-LB melting and/or
                          subsequent remelting and atomization. Even in nominally inert atmospheres, a residual
                        oxygen partial pressure is always present. At the temperatures involved in melt pool
                           formation and atomization, molten steel exhibits a strong chemical affinity for oxygen, al-
                          lowing selective oxidation to occur without noticeable nitrogen uptake. This interpretation
                                    is consistent with the observed dependence on atomization parameters: higher current,
                          corresponding to higher melt temperature, results in higher oxygen levels, while larger
                             vibration amplitude tends to reduce the oxygen content, likely due to shorter interaction
                          time between the liquid metal and the surrounding atmosphere. The presence of Mn-
                           Si-O enriched regions on some particle surfaces further supports oxygen fixation during
                                solidification after high-temperature exposure.
                                  Overall, the results indicate that the increase in oxygen content originates from selec-
                               tive high-temperature oxidation under non-ideal inert conditions. Even when processing
                                    is carried out in controlled atmospheres, a finite oxygen partial pressure remains and be-
                        comes thermodynamically significant at melting temperatures, leading to gradual oxygen




                                                                                                https://doi.org/10.3390/jmmp10030093J. Manuf. Mater. Process. 2026, 10, 93                                                                                             14 of 17



                          accumulation in the recycled material. This implies that in practical recycling routes, the
                        oxygen level should be considered a process-dependent parameter rather than a constant
                             material property. With repeated recycling cycles, the oxygen content is therefore expected
                               to increase at a diminishing rate and approach a quasi-steady level governed by the balance
                         between oxidation reactions and alloy deoxidation capacity. From an application perspec-
                                   tive, this behavior suggests that recycled powder does not necessarily need to be used as a
                            stand-alone feedstock: blending the secondary powder with lower-oxygen virgin powder
                    may provide a practical means of maintaining the oxygen content within specification
                               limits for demanding components while still enabling material reuse.
                           The increase in oxygen content after one recycling cycle also has implications for
                             further re-atomization. From a thermodynamic perspective, continuous linear oxygen
                          accumulation is unlikely, since oxidation during high-temperature processing is governed
                       by residual oxygen partial pressure and the alloy’s deoxidation capacity. After initial
                           oxidation and stabilization of oxide phases, the system is expected to approach a quasi-
                           equilibrium condition in which oxygen uptake is limited by process atmosphere and
                          melt chemistry. Consequently, subsequent recycling cycles would more likely lead to a
                           gradual stabilization of oxygen content rather than unlimited growth. This consideration is
                           important for evaluating the long-term viability of closed-loop powder recycling strategies.

                                   3.5. Efficiency of Ultrasonic Atomization

                           The efficiency of ultrasonic atomization was evaluated based on the yield of usable
                      powder as a function of two processing parameters: electric current and vibration ampli-
                            tude. As shown in Figure 9, the yield of usable powder ranges from 47% to 63%. The
                             highest yield (63%) was obtained at the minimum current of 70 A and the lowest vibration
                          amplitude of 60%. At amplitudes of 70% and 80%, the average yield gradually decreased.
                          For example, at 60% amplitude, the average yield for all samples was 59%; when at the
                          amplitudes of 70% and 80%, the average yields were 53% and 51%, respectively. As far as
                             the yield dependence on current is concerned, higher yield values tend to be achieved with
                            increased current.





                              Figure 9. Dependence of the yield on the current and the amplitude of ultrasonic vibrations.

                                  In addition, the stability of molten droplet formation prior to ultrasonic breakup plays
                        an important role in determining process efficiency. During preliminary observations, at
                             the lower boundary of the investigated current range, formation of relatively large molten




                                                                                                https://doi.org/10.3390/jmmp10030093J. Manuf. Mater. Process. 2026, 10, 93                                                                                             15 of 17



                            droplets was detected. Such droplets require sufficient vibrational energy to undergo
                              stable capillary-wave disintegration; otherwise, breakup may proceed in a less controlled
                        mode, reducing the fraction of usable powder. At elevated current values, increasing melt
                                fluidity may approach the limits of arc stability, which can also affect atomization behavior.
                             Therefore, the effective yield is governed by the existence of a stable operating window in
                        which droplet formation and capillary-wave breakup remain controlled.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Cemented carbides are essential in applications requiring exceptional hardness and wear resistance. However, the reliance on cobalt as a binder raises concerns related to cost, supply security, and health. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising cobalt-free binders offering favorable mechanical properties and potential grain-growth control. This work presents a new approach for the development of Co-free WC-based cemented carbide employing an HEA binder designed through CALPHAD-guided simulations. An optimized composition corresponding to Al5Cr5Cu10Fe35Mn10Ni35 (at%) alloy is predicted to be FCC-dominant with minimal σ-phase formation and good compatibility with WC. A preliminary batch of powder of the proposed binder was produced by blending elemental powders, arc remelting, and ultrasonic atomization, yielding predominantly spherical particles with a dendritic microstructure. WC–HEA composites (WC–12 wt% HEA) were then prepared by ball milling, pressing, vacuum sintering, and sinter-HIP for a first evaluation of the microstructure and achievable hardness. The microstructure exhibited residual porosity without significant WC grain coarsening. XRD analyses showed the dominant presence of WC, along with FCC and M3W3C phases (M mainly Fe and Mn), indicating thermal interaction between the binder and WC. Despite these effects, the composite achieved a hardness of 1913 HV and retained a fine WC grain size (0.86 μm). The proposed design approach allowed the definition of a promising Co-free binder composition based on HEA with the expected microstructure, which will need further evaluation, especially aimed at investigating toughness properties as a function of the WC content.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The quality and properties of metal powders are essential for powder metallurgical (PM) processes in general and for additive manufacturing (AM) processing routes in particular. Thus, a variety of atomization technologies were established meeting the multiple needs of the different processing technologies. However, the production of refractory metal alloy powder remains challenging due to their high liquidus temperatures (>2000 °C), the formation of brittle intermetallic phases, as well as the reactivity with and sensitivity to interstitials of the constituting elements. In this contribution, powders made of Mo-20Si-52.8-Ti (at.%) were produced by a novel ultrasonic atomization (UA) process at laboratory-scale using an industrial electrode induction gas atomization (EIGA) process with a modified electrode concept for the first time. UA allows flexibility in alloy composition due to the arc melting-based principle, while the EIGA electrode is PM manufactured from elemental powders to provide similar flexibility on a larger scale. The powders resulting from these two processes were compared with respect to size distribution, sphericity, microstructure and phase constitution, chemical composition, and interstitial impurity content. In addition, several powder batches were produced with the UA process in order to assess the process reliability and stability. The properties, quality, and quantities of UA powders perfectly meet the requests for alloy development for powder bed fusion AM, while the modified EIGA process allows the upscaling of the alloy powder quantities.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The demand for lightweight, high-performance, and multifunctional structures has driven rapid advances in multi-material joining technologies across aerospace, automotive, and electronics industries. Traditional joining methods often struggle with challenges such as thermal distortion, brittle intermetallic formation, and residual stresses when bonding dissimilar materials. This review critically examines three advanced additive manufacturing techniques—Ultrasonic Consolidation (UC), Cold Spray (CS), and Electron Beam Melting (EBM)—that offer promising solutions for multi-material fabrication. The mechanisms, material compatibility, microstructural evolution, and mechanical performance of joints produced by each process are systematically discussed. UC and CS, as solid-state processes, minimize thermal damage and oxidation, enabling strong joints between metals with dissimilar properties. EBM, operating in a high-vacuum environment, allows precise control over microstructure and enables the fabrication of complex, high-performance components. The novelty of this review lies in its integrative comparison of solid-state and fusion-based techniques, with a specific focus on their effectiveness in multi-material structural applications. It emphasizes interface behavior, residual stress development, and scalability challenges, while highlighting underexplored directions such as hybrid processing, interface engineering, tailored material feedstocks, and in-situ monitoring strategies. However, challenges such as bonding efficiency, residual stress management, and scalability remain. Future research directions are proposed, including process optimization, interface engineering, expanded material libraries, and integrated real-time monitoring to fully realize the potential of these emerging technologies for multi-material structural applications.</jats:p>

Three ultrasonic atomization (UA) powder batches, designated S1, S2, and S3, were produced and analyzed to assess process reliability and reproducibility. The batches showed good consistency in particle-size distribution: more than 85% of particles were between 40 and 80 µm, fewer than 6.4% were below 40 µm, and less than 0.2% were below 20 µm. Particle morphology was also consistent, with more than 90% of particles having an aspect ratio below 1.2, indicating good sphericity. ICP-OES found no significant batch-to-batch changes in alloy composition and no evidence of elemental vaporization during atomization. Oxygen content was the main compositional variation: S1 contained 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 contained 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm, and S3 contained 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm. The reported process yield was approximately 45–50 wt.% of the input rods converted into particles smaller than 100 µm.      2.2. Ultrasonic atomization powder production and atmosphere control

    Powders were prepared using an MSK-UP-300 ultrasonic atomization powder production system

with a nominal frequency of 35 kHz. The physical image of the equipment is shown in Fig. 1. The alloy

blocks were induction-heated in a heating crucible until completely molten. The melt was then guided

through a discharge valve onto the ultrasonic sonotrode, where it was disintegrated into droplets under

ultrasonic action and subsequently cooled and solidified to form powder. After the system cooled to room

temperature, the powder was collected, sieved through a 60-mesh standard sieve, and vacuum-sealed.





                                                4   Fig. 1 Physical image of the MSK-UP-300 ultrasonic atomization powder production system

    The experimental parameters were set as follows: ultrasonic amplitudes of 30%, 25%, and 20%;

melt heating temperatures of 199 °C – 499 °C; and sonotrode rotation speeds of 0 – 20 rpm. To investigate

the effect of a protective inert gas atmosphere on powder properties, argon was used as the protective

gas. Utilizing the property that argon is denser than air, a bottom-in, top-out gas flow mode was adopted.

Prior to the experiments, argon was pre-purged for 30 min to displace the air inside the chamber. The

experiments under the argon atmosphere were conducted using the optimal process parameters identified

from the experiments conducted in the air atmosphere.

     2.3. Solder paste formulation and ultrasonic-assisted soldering experiments

    The powders prepared under the optimal process parameters (amplitude: 30%, heating temperature:

199 °C, argon atmosphere) were uniformly mixed with a commercial flux to formulate the custom-made

solder paste. A commercial KZ-1513 Sn-58Bi solder paste was used as the control group. The solder

paste was evenly applied onto the pretreated copper surfaces, and the ultrasonic-assisted soldering was

performed on a constant-temperature heating platform at 170 °C. The ultrasonic soldering machine is

shown in Fig. 2. The soldering holding times were set to 10, 20, and 30 min, while the corresponding

ultrasonic durations were 2, 4, 8, and 16 s. Simultaneously, specimens without ultrasonic treatment were

prepared as blank controls.





                                                5                             Fig. 2 Handheld ultrasonic soldering machine

     2.4. Powder characterization and performance testing

    Micro-morphology and elemental analyses were conducted using a CLARA GMH field-emission

scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Tescan, Czech Republic) to observe the powder morphology

and the cross-sectional microstructure of the solder joints. The secondary electron (SE) mode was utilized

for powder characterization, the backscattered electron (BSE) mode for interfacial analysis, and the

equipped  energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)  for elemental  distribution mapping. The

volumetric particle size parameters (D10, D50, and D90) were determined using a Bettersize 2600 laser

diffraction particle size analyzer (Dandong Bettersize, China). Prior to the measurements, the samples

were ultrasonically dispersed for 10 min. The sphericity and satellite index of the powders were evaluated

using an R-3000 particle size and shape analyzer (Micro-Spectrum Technology, China). The oxygen

content was measured with an ONH-3500 oxygen/nitrogen/hydrogen elemental analyzer (NCS Testing

Technology, China). The melt contact angles were measured using a DSAHT 1600 high-temperature

contact angle meter (KRÜSS, Germany) on a substrate made of the same titanium alloy as the sonotrode.

The measurements were performed in both air and argon atmospheres after isothermally holding the

samples for 10 min at various temperature points ranging from 199 to 499 °C. The dynamic viscosity of

the melt within the temperature range of 199–499 °C was tested using a BCT-1700 high-temperature

viscometer (Huanao Technology, China).

     2.5. Evaluation of interfacial metallurgy and shear mechanical properties

    The soldered joints were cross-sectioned, ground, and polished. Subsequently, they were etched

with a 4 wt.% hydrochloric acid-ethanol solution for 5 s. The morphology of the intermetallic compounds

(IMCs) was observed, and their thickness was measured using the BSE mode of the FE-SEM. The shear

strength of the joints was evaluated using a WDW-50A electronic universal testing machine (Xinguang

                                                6Testing Machine, China) at a crosshead speed of 0.5 mm/min. To ensure data reliability, 3 to 5 specimens

were tested for each set of parameters.


     3. Results and discussion

     3.1. Effect of ultrasonic amplitude on powder properties





      Fig. 3 SEM images of Sn-58Bi powders under different ultrasonic amplitudes: (a) 30%; (b)

                               25%; (c) 20%

     Fig. 3 shows the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images of the Sn-58Bi powders prepared at

different ultrasonic amplitudes. As the ultrasonic amplitude increased from 20% to 30%, the proportion

of spherical powders gradually increased, while the amount of irregular powders [13] and satellite

particles [8] progressively decreased. At an amplitude of 30%, the powders exhibited the highest quantity

of spherical particles with smooth surfaces and few satellites; conversely, at 20% amplitude, abundant

irregular particles and satellites emerged.





                                                7  Fig. 4 Particle size distributions of Sn-58Bi powders under different ultrasonic amplitudes: (a)

                   30%; (b) 25%; (c) 20%; (d) D10, D50, and D90

     Fig. 4 illustrates the particle size distributions of the Sn-58Bi powders prepared at different

ultrasonic amplitudes. The particle size under each amplitude exhibited a unimodal normal distribution,

although the peak position and width varied. When the ultrasonic amplitude was 30%, the D10, volumetric

median diameter D50, and D90 of the powders were 39.08 μm, 83.37 μm, and 198.2 μm, respectively, all

of which were smaller than the corresponding values at amplitudes of 25% and 20%. The span S was

employed to quantify the width of the particle size distribution [10, 14]: S= D90-D10 . The S values at
                                                                                        D50

amplitudes of 30% and 25% were close, being 1.909 and 1.911, respectively. However, at 20%, the S

value increased to 2.079, indicating that a lower amplitude leads to a broader particle size distribution.





                                                8  Fig. 5 Sphericity and satellite index of Sn-58Bi powders under different ultrasonic amplitudes

     Fig. 5 presents the sphericity and satellite index of the powders prepared at different ultrasonic

amplitudes. As the ultrasonic amplitude increased, the sphericity gradually increased, while the satellite

index progressively decreased. At an amplitude of 30%, the sphericity reached its maximum and the

satellite index its minimum, indicating that this amplitude facilitates the shrinkage of droplets into

spheres and suppresses the formation of satellite particles [15].

    The above phenomena can be explained by the capillary wave mechanism of ultrasonic atomization

[16, 17]. As the driving amplitude increases, the amplitude of the capillary waves also increases. When

the wave amplitude exceeds a critical threshold, the wave surface becomes unstable, and droplets detach

from the wave crests, initiating atomization [18]. A higher amplitude accelerates the growth of capillary

waves and shortens the time required for the liquid film to reach the critical breakup thickness, thereby

resulting in the formation of finer droplets from the melt. In addition to the capillary wave effect,

cavitation  is another  crucial mechanism through which  ultrasonic amplitude influences powder

properties. In an ultrasonic field, tiny gas nuclei within the liquid undergo oscillation, expansion, and

contraction under the action of acoustic waves, ultimately leading to implosion [19]. When the ultrasonic

amplitude increases, the amplitude of the acoustic pressure injected into the melt correspondingly rises.

Consequently, a massive number of cavitation bubbles rapidly expand and aggregate into bubble clusters

during the negative pressure phase. Upon collapsing during the high-pressure phase, these bubbles

generate micro-shock waves and microjets that tear the liquid film from within. This internal tearing

synergizes with the surface capillary wave instability to form a cooperative fragmentation mechanism

[20, 21]. An increase in the driving acoustic pressure leads to an elevated bubble number density, which

intensifies the coupling interactions among the bubbles and exacerbates the c

ely leading to implosion [19]. When the ultrasonic

amplitude increases, the amplitude of the acoustic pressure injected into the melt correspondingly rises.

Consequently, a massive number of cavitation bubbles rapidly expand and aggregate into bubble clusters

during the negative pressure phase. Upon collapsing during the high-pressure phase, these bubbles

generate micro-shock waves and microjets that tear the liquid film from within. This internal tearing

synergizes with the surface capillary wave instability to form a cooperative fragmentation mechanism

[20, 21]. An increase in the driving acoustic pressure leads to an elevated bubble number density, which

intensifies the coupling interactions among the bubbles and exacerbates the cavitation effect [22].

                                                9     Therefore, increasing the amplitude not only enhances the capillary wave effect but also intensifies

the fragmentation of the liquid film caused by cavitation implosions. Together, these two mechanisms

result in droplet refinement and a reduction in powder particle size. Consequently, under the present

experimental conditions, an amplitude of 30% is conducive to obtaining finer and more uniformly sized

Sn-58Bi powders.

     3.2. Effect of melt heating temperature on powder properties

     3.2.1. Powder morphology and particle size distribution





  Fig. 6 SEM images of Sn-58Bi powders at different melt heating temperatures: (a) 199 °C; (b)

                   259 °C; (c) 319 °C; (d) 379 °C; (e) 439 °C; (f) 499 °C

     Fig. 6 shows the morphology of the Sn-58Bi powders prepared  at  different melt heating

temperatures. As the heating temperature increased from 199 °C to 499 °C, the proportion of regular

spherical  particles  decreased,  while  irregular  particles and  inter-particle  adhesion phenomena

significantly increased, accompanied by a rise in the number of satellite particles. Overall, the sphericity

of fine particles was superior to that of coarse particles.





                                               10 Fig. 7 Particle size distributions of Sn-58Bi powders at different melt heating temperatures: (a)

              199 °C; (b) 259 °C; (c) 319 °C; (d) 379 °C; (e) 439 °C; (f) 499 °C

     Fig. 7 presents the particle size distribution curves of the powders at different melt heating

temperatures, with all samples exhibiting unimodal normal distribution characteristics. The particle size

parameters are listed in Table 1. As the heating temperature rose, the median diameter D50 initially

decreased and then increased, reaching a minimum value of 91.6 μm at 259 °C. The D50 was 92.5 μm at

199 °C, increased continuously beyond 319 °C, and rose to 106.3 μm at 499 °C. The span S was generally

maintained between 1.7 and 2.2. Specifically, at 319 °C, S reached its minimum of 1.7, indicating the

most concentrated particle size distribution. At 439 °C and 499 °C, S rose to 2.2, reflecting a broadened

distribution.

empirical equation [23, 24]: σm ( M   3                               ρm)  =K(Tc-T), where σ  is the surface tension, M  is the molar mass
of the melt, ρm  is the melt density, Tc  is the melting point, and K  is an experimental constant.

According to this equation, the surface tension of the metal melt is negatively correlated with temperature.

                                                                                                                1
Furthermore, based on the droplet size estimation formula [25]: Dp=0.34 ( 8πσm ) 3 , where Dp  is the                                                                                                                   ρf2

droplet size, σm  is the surface tension, ρ  is the liquid density, and  f  is the frequency. By combining

these two equations, it can be deduced that as the temperature rises and surface tension decreases, the

atomized droplet size should theoretically continue to decrease, and the droplets should find it more

     3.2.2. Melt viscosity and powder oxygen content

    To elucidate the anomalous variation in particle size, the dynamic viscosity of the Sn-58Bi melt and

the oxygen content of the corresponding powders were measured at different temperatures, as shown in

Fig. 8(a) and (b). The viscosity test results indicate that the melt viscosity exhibits a declining trend as

the temperature rises. It should be noted that the overall viscosity values measured in the air atmosphere

are somewhat high. This is attributed to the oxide film formed on the melt surface, which hinders the

rotation of the viscometer rotor [27]. Nevertheless, the fundamental rule that viscosity decreases with

increasing temperature remains unaffected.





 Fig. 8 Effect of melt temperature on Sn-58Bi powder characteristics: (a) dynamic viscosity of the

             melt; (b) oxygen content distribution; (c) sphericity and satellite index

    The powder oxygen content also exhibits a trend of initially decreasing and then increasing with the

heating temperature. The extremum point coincides with that of the particle size, both occurring at 259 °C.

This variation likely stems from the competition between two mechanisms: (1) When the temperature is

below 259 °C, the viscosity reduction induced by the temperature rise plays a dominant role. The lower-
                                               12viscosity melt spreads more readily on the sonotrode to form a thin liquid film, thereby enhancing the

ultrasonic atomization  efficiency. Consequently, the powder  particle  size gradually  refines with

increasing temperature, which is consistent with theoretical predictions. (2) When the temperature

exceeds 259 °C, the high-temperature oxidation effect gradually becomes the dominant factor. Surface

oxidation of the melt intensifies, forming an oxide film. During ultrasonic fragmentation, this oxide film

breaks up alongside the droplets and adheres to the particle surfaces, leading to an increase in particle

size [28]. Simultaneously, the reduced surface tension prolongs the spheroidization time of the droplets.

Droplets that have not fully solidified are more prone to colliding and coalescing during flight, further

resulting in a higher proportion of coarse particles and an overall increase in particle size.

     3.2.3. Sphericity and satellite index

    The sphericity and satellite index of the powders at different temperatures are shown in Fig. 8(c).

As the melt heating temperature rises, the sphericity decreases, and the satellite index increases. At

199 °C, the sphericity reaches its peak, and satellite particles are minimized. This trend is consistent with

the relationship between surface tension and temperature. Surface tension acts as the driving force for

the droplet spheroidization process, functioning to minimize the surface area of the liquid mass. However,

the elevated temperature lowers the surface tension, resulting in insufficient spheroidization driving force.

Consequently,  it becomes more difficult for the droplets to shrink into regular spheres, making the

formation of irregular powders more likely at higher temperatures.

     3.3. Effect of inert protective atmosphere on powder properties

    Abstract
    Current methods for the production of spherical powders restrict the development of new chemical compositions dedicated to the
    additive manufacturing industry. This novel ultrasonic atomization process enables in-house powder production from even one gram
   up to a few kilograms to verify new alloys. The technology use vibrations to break the surface tension of liquid metal to allow
    atomization. To melt the material plasma torch or induction heating can be used allowing to process wide range of metals.
    Plasma-based ultrasonic atomization was used to manufacture spherical powder of a high-temperature alloy, while induction-based
    ultrasonic atomization was used to develop a low-melting alloy. Additional case study of recycling titanium alloy maching chips into
    the powder by arc melting and ultrasonic atomization is presented.

   Keywords: Ultrasonic atomization, alloy development, additive manufacturing, custom powder production, recycling

    Introduction
    Metal powders are widely used in novel production methods, like laser powder bed fusion1), electron beam melting2), or direct energy
    deposition3). Additive manufacturing often requires materials with high flowability, and high packing density resulting in the need for
    spherical powders. The morphology limits the number of powder manufacturing methods that can be used for these processes. The
  AM industry mainly uses powders obtained by gas atomization4), water atomization5), and plasma/induction spheroidization6). These
    technologies allow for mass-production of powders. However, they are not conducive alloy development in AM due to costs
    associated with production changeover, requirements for specific feedstock types, and space requirements which do not allow the
     installation of such systems at research institutes or Universities. This results in the necessity to use powder blends7) or non-spherical
    powders8) influencing the homogeneity of chemical composition, and flowability.

    Ultrasonic atomization solves this issue thanks to the usage of vibration to break the surface tension of liquid metal to form droplets
     that solidify in a free-flow manner9). The absence of a high-velocity fluid stream such as in gas or water atomization allows for
    scaling down the atomization chamber. The ability for the melting mechanism to produce liquid metal in the moment of contact with
    the sonotrode allows it to work with any feedstock type without interfering with alloy development due to the complex process of
    feedstock preparation, like powder10) or wire11). Ultrasonic atomization was successfully used to obtain custom powders with tailored
    chemical composition: Zr-based alloy for bulk metallic glass formation during laser powder bed fusion12), platinum-based superalloy
    Pt84-Al11-Cr3-Ru2 for high-temperature applications13), AZ31B magnesium alloy modified with lithium to reduce its density14),
   aluminum 5754 alloy for automotive industry15), as well as functional material like Ni-Mn-Ga Heusler alloy with magnetocaloric
     properties16).

   C103 is a refractory-based niobium alloy for high-temperature applications like rocket propulsion systems and hypersonic missiles.
   The first use of this alloy was in Apollo Lunar Command Module rocket nozzles. Due to its main usage as thin-walled geometries
    and hard-to-machine nature, the examination of its usability in AM was launched. It was found that additively manufactured C103
    can achieve properties at ambient and 1093°C temperature required by ASTM B655 and can surpass the ultimate tensile strength of
     its wrought counterpart17).

   Magnesium alloys are extensively studied for orthopedic implants, which do not require removal thanks to their biodegradable
    properties without toxic ion release that can cause metallosis18). To adjust their corrosion rate to the bone tissue healing rate elements
     like silver can be used which additionally can result in an antibacterial effect of the lattice structures19).

    Titanium alloys are commonly used in aviation and aerospace application due to their high strength to weight ratio. Close loop of
    such materials is critical for sustainable research, especially concerning their strategic usage.

    In this article, ultrasonic atomization results of niobium C103 (Nb-10Hf-1Ti) alloy, magnesium alloy modified with silver and
    recycling of the titanium machining chips will be presented.

    Experimental
    Ultrasonic atomization was carried out on rePOWDER (Amazemet, Poland). C103 niobium alloy was atomized from narrow sheet
     strips using a TZM rod sonotrode with a diameter of 30 mm which vibrated with a 40 kHz frequency. The ultrasonic vibrations,
    delivered through a sonotrode, create a standing wave on the surface of the sonotrode, which is transferred to the molten metal. By
    reaching the threshold amplitude, the internal forces of the liquid are broken, ejecting droplets of molten metal that solidify in an
    argon atmosphere. The chamber in which atomization was conducted is presented in Figure 1.

   was poured by the over-pressure control of argon after lifting the sealing rod, which was closing the nozzle opening. The stream of

    alloy which caused mist formation in the chamber (Figure 2A) induction-based ultrasonic atomization of copper alloy is presented in

    Conclusions

     •   Ultrasonic atomization allows to obtain C103 niobium alloy with homogenous structure and morphology beneficial for additive
    manufacturing.
     •  When selecting the pouring temperature of Mg alloy during induction-based ultrasonic atomization possible evaporation of zinc
    and particle bonding must be considered.
     •  rePOWDER thanks to arc melting and ultrasonic atomization modules allow to recycling scraps
    of strategic materials like titanium alloy. As-atomized powder have narrow PSD which is suitable for additive manufacturing and
    other powder metallurgy methods.

   The ownership structure of a mining company can impact its risk tolerance and the environments in which it
    operates. SOEs may be more willing to invest in riskier environments that publicly listed companies may avoid.
   A notable example of this are Chinese SOEs, which have a significant presence in Africa’s mining industry, including
     in countries where risks, real or perceived, may deter other investors (Ayuk et al., 2020).

   Some of the largest companies in the mineral and metal industry value chain are vertically integrated, meaning
    they operate across multiple stages of the value chain (e.g. BHP, Rio Tinto and Freeport-McMoRan). Other
    companies specialise in specific stages. For instance, some specialise in mineral extraction but do not have the
     facilities to process or refine them. Other companies specialise in refining raw materials into metals but do not have
    the facilities to mine or process minerals. Many recycling companies specialise in collecting and processing specific
    types of waste materials rather than operating across the other parts of value chains.

   The energy transition is changing corporate strategies and value chains in the mining industry. For instance, BHP,
    the world’s largest mining company by market capitalisation, is divesting its oil and gas business and positioning
     itself as a mining company focused on the energy transition (Quiggin, 2021). The growing demand for critical
    materials is also attracting companies from outside of the traditional mining industry. Tesla, an EV manufacturer,
      is building a lithium refinery in Texas and is looking to expand its footprint in the minerals mining and processing
    business (Agatie, 2023). Some mining companies are keen to invest in new businesses linked to the energy
     transition. For example, the Fortescue Metals Group has created a new unit to invest in renewables, green
    hydrogen and green ammonia.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Nickel–titanium (NiTi) shape memory alloys offer transformative functionality for biomedical and aerospace systems, yet their adoption in additive manufacturing (AM) remains constrained by powder reactivity, compositional sensitivity, and the high energy of feedstock production. This work establishes a unified, data-driven evaluation of how powder-state evolution during reuse and ultrasonic plasma atomization (UPA) affects both functional behavior and environmental performance. Virgin, reused, and UPA-recycled NiTi powders were systematically characterized based on particle-size distribution (PSD), SEM morphology, sphericity, oxygen content (ONH), and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and these results were coupled with a process-level life-cycle assessment (LCA) spanning cradle-to-gate feedstock generation. Reused powder showed finer but broadened PSD, surface oxidation, and elevated transformation temperatures; these degradation mechanisms limited its reuse despite reducing energy demand by ~30% relative to virgin powder. UPA provided a more effective regeneration pathway: UPA-recycled NiTi recovered high sphericity and smooth particle surfaces while lowering cradle-to-gate energy from 100 ± 10 to 50 ± 5 MJ·kg−1 (≈50%) and reducing CO2-equivalent emissions by ≈45%, with ~95% material recovery. Although the UPA condition exhibited a higher oxygen content in this study due to system-level atmosphere limitations, prior work indicates that optimized inert-gas control can suppress oxidation, suggesting clear avenues for improvement. Sustainability Index analysis confirmed UPA as the most favorable route, integrating reductions in energy demand and emissions with recovery of powder morphology and reconditioning of thermal transformation behavior. More broadly, the ability of UPA to promote compositional and microstructural redistribution highlights its potential to deliberately re-tune or “reprogram” transformation temperatures for application-specific requirements when alloying and processing atmospheres are carefully managed.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>In this paper, a detailed assessment of Inconel 718 powder, with varying degrees of degradation due to repeated use in the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) process, has been undertaken. Four states of IN718 powder (virgin, used, overflow and spatter) were characterized in terms of their morphology, flowability and physico-chemical properties. Studies showed that used and overflow powders were almost identical. The fine particle-size distribution of the virgin powder, in which 50% of particles were found to be below the nominal particle-size distribution (PSD), was recognized as the main reason for its lower flowability and the main cause of the differentiation between virgin, used and overflow powders. Only spatter powder was found to be degraded enough to preclude its direct LPBF reuse. The oxygen content in the spatter powder exceeded the limit value for IN718 by 290 ppm, and aluminum oxide spots were found on the spatter particles surfaces. Laser absorption analysis showed 10 pp higher laser absorption compared to the other powders. The results of evaluation showed that IN718 powder is resistant to multiple uses in the LPBF process. Due to the low degradation rate of IN718 powder, overflow powder can be re-enabled for multiple uses with a proper recycling strategy.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Shape memory alloys (SMAs) are transformative materials renowned for their ability to reversibly change shape in response to thermal and mechanical stimuli. While nitinol (NiTi) remains the most extensively studied SMA, a growing portfolio of alternative systems, particularly copper-based alloys, offer compelling advantages in cost, durability, and functional versatility. These materials are increasingly vital in demanding environments requiring high performance, corrosion resistance, and tailored thermomechanical behavior. Recent breakthroughs in additive manufacturing, especially laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), have revolutionized the fabrication of complex SMA components, enabling unprecedented microstructural control, intricate architectures, and customized properties. This review synthesizes cutting-edge research on LPBF processing of diverse SMA systems, emphasizing how process parameters influence phase transformations, microstructural evolution, defect formation, and functional stability. It explores innovative structural designs, such as lattice and auxetic configurations, that unlock new levels of performance in biomedical devices, aerospace actuators, and energy absorption systems. Despite significant progress, challenges such as residual stresses, material homogeneity, and scalability continue to hinder widespread deployment. This review highlights promising avenues for future research: optimizing alloy compositions, refining processing techniques, and expanding application horizons. By advancing our understanding of microstructure-property relationships, these efforts aim to unlock the full potential of both traditional and emerging SMAs across a broad spectrum of industries.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Throughout recent years, the implementation of nanoparticles into the microstructure of additively manufactured (AM) parts has gained great attention in the material science community. The dispersion strengthening (DS) effect achieved leads to a substantial improvement in the mechanical properties of the alloy used. In this work, an ex situ approach of powder conditioning prior to the AM process as per a newly developed fluidized bed reactor (FBR) was applied to a titanium-enriched variant of the NiCu-based Alloy 400. Powders were investigated before and after FBR exposure, and it was found that the conditioning led to a significant increase in the TiN formation along grain boundaries. Manufactured to parts via laser-based powder bed fusion of metals (PBF-LB/M), the ex situ FBR approach not only revealed a superior microstructure compared to unconditioned parts but also with respect to a recently introduced in situ approach based on a gas atomization reaction synthesis (GARS). A substantially higher number of nanoparticles formed along cell walls and enabled an effective suppression of dislocation movement, resulting in excellent tensile, creep, and fatigue properties, even at elevated temperatures up to 750 °C. Such outstanding properties have never been documented for AM-processed Alloy 400, which is why the demonstrated FBR ex situ conditioning marks a promising modification route for future alloy systems.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000032

From text 'yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3'.

Andrei Yankin, Hussain Ali Murtaza, Boris Golman, Asma Perveen, and Didier Talamona. Effect of ultrasonic atomization parameters on alsi12 aluminum powder characteristics for additive manufacturing. Scientific Reports, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7. This article has 5 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt reports that approximately 75% of the powder produced by ultrasonic atomization was converted into powder usable for the laboratory’s Renishaw AM400 selective laser melting system, because only particles smaller than 63 μm were accepted. This is the only yield or AM-suitable fraction explicitly stated in the provided pages. The excerpt does not provide numerical sphericity values or a satellite-particle fraction; those metrics may be reported elsewhere in the article. The process variables investigated as likely sources of powder-characteristic variability were electrical current, ultrasonic vibration amplitude, and electric-arc (torch) position. The operating matrix used 140 or 150 A current, 75% or 80% vibration amplitude, and torch positions from −5° to +5°, at a fixed 35 kHz frequency. Current and amplitude were first varied to identify settings based on rheological properties, after which the torch position was optimized. These variables were evaluated for their effects on powder morphology, particle-size distribution, and rheological behavior.

This article has 0 citations.

The excerpt reports an average sphericity of 0.94 for niobium powder produced by ultrasonic atomization. It describes the ultrasonic-atomized particles as nearly perfectly spherical, clean, and free from satellites, agglomerates, inclusions, surface irregularities, shrinkage patterns, folding, and oxidation-related defects. However, no numerical satellite fraction is provided; the text only states that satellites were absent or not observed. The reported particle-size distribution is approximately 44–67 μm (D10 = 44.12 μm, D50 = 54.99 μm, and D90 = 66.85 μm), and this fraction is considered suitable for several additive-manufacturing applications, particularly electron-beam PBF systems operating around 45–100 μm. The excerpt notes that the powder is at the coarse end of laser-PBF specifications, while finer fractions of roughly 15–45 μm can be produced using higher ultrasonic frequencies for conventional LPBF or applications requiring better surface quality and resolution. A numerical powder-yield value is not reported in the supplied pages. The excerpt also does not explicitly identify dominant sources of process variability; it mentions lower ultrasonic frequency, droplet volume, resonant excitation, cooling conditions, and model assumptions such as thermal gradients and transient instabilities as relevant process factors.

Scientific Reports, Jul 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7, doi:10.1038/s41598-025-06086-7. This article has 5 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt does not provide exact numerical values for ultrasonic-atomization powder yield, sphericity, or satellite fraction. It does report that more than half of the UA-produced batch met AM requirements, which is the only explicit indication of the AM-suitable powder fraction in this passage. It also states that UA powder had a suitability factor 21% higher than commercial powder and exhibited improved sphericity relative to the irregular, fused particles found in commercial alternatives. The excerpt does not quantify the sphericity values or satellite fraction. The investigated process variables were arc manipulator angle, electrical current, and vibration amplitude. Among these, electrical current was identified as the dominant source of variability in powder quality, followed by arc angle and vibration amplitude. Parameter changes produced particle-size-distribution span variations of up to 37.5%. The reported optimum combination for rheological properties was increased vibration amplitude from 75% to 80%, reduced arc angle from 5° to −5°, and reduced current from 150 A to 140 A. Powder suitability also showed a nonlinear dependence on arc angle, worsening sharply above 0°.

Materials, 17:5642, Nov 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/ma17225642, doi:10.3390/ma17225642. This article has 11 citations.

The excerpt does not report the numerical powder yield, sphericity values, satellite fraction, or AM-suitable powder fraction. The process variables explicitly varied in the experimental plan were torch current, from 70 to 150 A, and wire feed speed, from 35% to 60% (equivalent to 6.83–28.77 mm/s). Argon flow was held constant at 60%, ultrasonic-wave amplitude at 80%, and the atomization time at 60 minutes; the ultrasound frequency ranged from 35.0 to 35.3 kHz. The excerpt indicates that process instability was associated with unsuitable parameter combinations, particularly wire feed speeds that were too high or current levels that were too low. Five runs—S5, S9, S10, S13, and S14—were discontinued because of high instability and excluded from further testing. Thus, based on the provided pages, current and wire feed speed are the principal investigated sources of variability, while the specific reported powder-performance metrics would need to be obtained from later sections of the article.

The supplied excerpt reports that ultrasonic-atomized 316L powder had sphericity coefficients ranging from 0.84 to 0.90, compared with an average sphericity of 0.56 for virgin powder. It describes the ultrasonic powder as having smooth surfaces and a minimal number of satellites, but no numerical satellite fraction is provided in these pages. Likewise, powder yield and the fraction classified as suitable for additive manufacturing (AM) are not reported in the supplied excerpt, so those values would need to be obtained from other pages or tables of the article. Regarding process variability, the excerpt discusses electric current and vibration amplitude as the principal investigated atomization variables. Their effect on the cumulative particle-size distribution was generally limited, although a deviation at 70% vibration amplitude was attributed to a transition between atomization conditions. More broadly, variability in surface morphology and composition is linked to atomization intensity, capillary-wave and cavitation behavior, droplet thermal history, cooling/solidification time, and oxidation kinetics. Higher amplitude can intensify cavitation and capillary waves, while larger particles retain liquid instabilities longer and develop stronger surface relief. The excerpt does not establish a quantified ranking of dominant variables for yield, satellite fraction, or AM-suitable fraction.

Journal of Achievements in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering, 116:11-24, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393, doi:10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393. This article has 38 citations.

The excerpt reports an ultrasonic atomization conversion rate above 95% and, after improvements to the gas-flow design, recovery of more than 98% useful powder from the feedstock. It does not provide the specific sphericity values, satellite fraction, or additive-manufacturing-suitable powder fraction requested. The process variability discussed is primarily associated with gas-flow behavior and droplet trajectories: low-kinetic-energy droplets in low-density Ti alloys can be deflected by gas turbulence and remain in stagnation zones, adhering to chamber walls rather than reaching powder separation. The sonotrode also ejects droplets stochastically, with variation in direction and diameter. Differences in droplet kinetic energy can produce inter-droplet collisions and reduce powder sphericity. CFD analysis was used to identify gas-flow, turbulence, thermal, and stagnation zones, and to optimize the velocity profile and downstream gas-flow features. Other reported operating variables include ultrasonic frequency (35 kHz), chamber pressure (approximately 1.1 bar), argon atmosphere, arc current (130 A), and molten-metal temperature maintained at roughly 1.3–1.5 times the liquidus.

The dominant process/material variables identified are ultrasonic frequency, energy distribution, liquid density, surface tension, and vibration amplitude; these govern capillary wavelength and droplet separation. The excerpt also notes that raw-material composition affects the resulting powder. Surface defects, bumps, and protrusions were observed and said to impair uniform powder layering and flow, but no satellite fraction was quantified.

function.arguments: {"question": "What is the powder output yield suitable for additive manufacturing from \u017brodowski cold crucible ultrasonic atomization? What D10, D50, D90, and sphericity values were reported for the metallic glass and other alloys?"}
function.name: gather_evidence

messages.content:
Most relevant evidence (with ids):

## pqac-00000043

From text 'ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6'.

Jakub Ciftcli, Tomasz Choma, Bartosz Morończyk, Bartosz Kalicki, Filip Puchalski, and Łukasz Żrodowski. Alloy development from sustainable materials – close-loop of materials using ultrasonic atomization. Journal of the Japan Society of Powder and Powder Metallurgy, 72:S729-S735, Mar 2025. URL: https://doi.org/10.2497/jjspm.15e-sis13-03, doi:10.2497/jjspm.15e-sis13-03. This article has 7 citations.

The excerpt identifies the cold-crucible/plasma-melted, ultrasonic-atomized Ti alloy made from recycled CNC machining chips as the relevant Żrodowski process. More than 85% of the atomized Ti powder was below 100 µm, a fraction stated to be suitable for laser powder bed fusion and other powder-based manufacturing methods. The reported particle-size distribution depends on the analysis method: volume-based D10, D50, and D90 were 36, 49, and 118 µm, respectively; number-based values were 30, 41, and 52 µm, respectively. The excerpt reports high sphericity for the Ti powder but does not provide a numerical sphericity value. For the niobium C103 alloy, it describes spherical morphology, a narrow particle-size distribution, and a high sphericity factor, again without a numerical sphericity value. The magnesium-silver alloy is described as having a desired particle-size distribution, but no D10/D50/D90 or numerical sphericity data are given. No metallic-glass results or corresponding metallic-glass sphericity values appear in the supplied pages, so those values cannot be recovered from this excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000044

From text 'scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8'.

International Scientific, B. Bałasz, M. Bielecki, W. Gulbiński, and Ł. Słoboda. Comparison of ultrasonic and other atomization methods in metal powder production. Journal of Achievements in Materials and Manufacturing Engineering, 116:11-24, Jan 2023. URL: https://doi.org/10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393, doi:10.5604/01.3001.0016.3393. This article has 38 citations.

The excerpt reports that the cold-crucible ultrasonic atomization system recovered more than 98% of useful powder from the feedstock, indicating a high powder-output yield. For the Ti6Al4V production-scale example, a powder batch classified at 63 ± 20 μm had particle-size values of D10 = 40.2 μm, D50 = 52.0 μm, and D90 = 60.8 μm when based on particle counting. The corresponding volume-percentile values were D10 = 45.4 μm, D50 = 55.0 μm, and D90 = 62.4 μm. The excerpt also gives comparison data for MetcoAdd powder: optical particle-count measurements produced D10 = 16.1 μm, D50 = 31.0 μm, and D90 = 53.4 μm; volume-percentile processing gave D10 = 29.0 μm, D50 = 47.3 μm, and D90 = 77.8 μm. Although the question asks about metallic glass and other alloys, the supplied pages only describe Ti6Al4V and a commercial-powder comparison. They do not report metallic-glass-specific particle sizes or any numerical sphericity values. The passage notes that droplet collisions can reduce powder sphericity, but no measured sphericity result is included.

{"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive summary table of all published ultrasonic atomization (UA) data relevant to repeatability. Include columns for: Reference, Alloy, Equipment/Frequency, Number of batches/replicates, D10/D50/D90 (µm), Span, Yield (%), Sphericity, Oxygen content, and whether true replicate data exist. Include all studies found:

1. Hinrichs 2021: Mo-20Si-52.8Ti, 3DLab ATO, 3 batches (S1-S3), >85% in 40-80µm, d90 values 63/72/78 µm across batches, >90% AR<1.2, O: 1450±20/1330±10/1280±30 ppm, yield 45-50% (<100µm). TRUE REPLICATE DATA.

2. Yankin 2025: AlSi12, 3DLab ATO 35kHz, 7 parameter conditions (not replicates), D10 38.7-44.7, D50 52.3-54.7, D90 66.4-72.7, span 0.40-0.64, yield ~75% (<63µm). No SD/CV reported.

3. Bashmakova 2026: 316L SS (recycled), 35kHz, 18 conditions (3 rods each), d10 12-15, d50 23-34, d90 45-49, span 1.00-1.46, sphericity 0.84-0.90, yield 47-63%, O increase observed.

4. Bałasz et al. 2023: Ti6Al4V, 35kHz, 2 batches, D10=40.2, D50=52.0, D90=60.8 (count) for classified batch, >94% conversion, 70.3% in 63±20µm, sphericity 0.88-0.90.

5. Wróbel 2026: Nb, 35kHz, single batch, D10=44.12, D50=54.99, D90=66.85, span=0.413, sphericity 0.94.

6. Yang 2026: Sn-58Bi, 35kHz, parameter study, D50=65.5-106.3µm varying with T, sphericity 0.87, satellite index 1.07 at optimal.

7. Ciftci 2025 (AMAZEMET rePowder): C103 Nb, Ti alloy (recycled), Mg-Ag; 40kHz and 60kHz. Ti: vol D10/D50/D90 = 36/49/118, >85% <100µm, O pickup ~220 ppm.

8. Halapi 2023: 17-4PH and 1.4551 SS, sieve fractions only, no PSD metrics, no replicates."}

1. Ultrasonic frequency (35-60 kHz range): Doubling frequency reduces particle size ~40%, strongest theoretical control. Bałasz 2023.
2. Vibration amplitude: Higher amplitude -> finer droplets, higher sphericity, lower satellite index, but yield may decrease. Yankin 2025 (3rd ranked effect), Bashmakova 2026 (yield decreased from 59% to 51% as amplitude increased 60->80%), Yang 2026 (amplitude 30% best sphericity=0.87).
3. Electrical current / arc power: Strongest observed effect (Yankin 2025, ranked #1). Affects melt superheat and flow. Higher current -> broader PSD in some cases, higher yield at higher current (Bashmakova), but can cause arc instability. D10 and D50 significantly decreased at 150A vs 140A (Yankin).
4. Arc/torch angle or position: Non-linear effect, sharp worsening above 0° (Yankin 2025, ranked #2).
5. Melt superheat/temperature: Affects surface tension, viscosity, oxidation. Competing mechanisms: lower viscosity -> finer particles, but higher T -> more oxidation -> coarser particles. Yang 2026 found D50 minimum at 259°C for Sn-58Bi.
6. Wire feed rate / melt flow rate: Too high -> process instability (Bałasz 2024, 5 of 16 runs failed). Must match melting capacity.
7. Sonotrode material and temperature / wetting: Affects melt spreading, contact angle; Ar atmosphere reduces contact angle (Yang 2026). Sonotrode contamination is a known risk.
8. Atmosphere / oxygen partial pressure: Ar vs air affects oxidation, particle size, sphericity. Bashmakova 2026 and Yang 2026 report oxygen-dependent behavior.
9. Gas flow pattern in chamber: Affects droplet trajectory, recovery, collisions; CFD-optimized flow improved yield >98% (Bałasz 2023)."}

{"answer": "# Run-to-Run Repeatability of Ultrasonic Atomization of Molten Metals: A Critical Review of Published Data

## Overview and Key Finding

**True fixed-setting, batch-to-batch replicate data for ultrasonic atomization (UA) of molten metals are extremely scarce in the open literature.** After a comprehensive search across journal publications and patents covering sonotrode/vibrating-plate UA systems (including AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO, and lab-built 20–60 kHz systems), only one study — Hinrichs et al. (2021) on Mo–20Si–52.8Ti — explicitly produced and compared multiple powder batches at nominally identical process settings to assess reproducibility. All other studies report single batches or parameter-variation campaigns that can only serve as proxies for process variability. No published data were found for true replicate runs on aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, Scalmalloy) or any other alloy system beyond the Mo-Si-Ti case. The following sections present what numerical data exist, organized by the requested categories.

The table below summarizes all published UA datasets with their available repeatability information or closest proxies:

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

## (a) Spread in Particle Size Distribution Across Replicate Runs

**True replicate data exist only for one alloy system.** Hinrichs et al. (2021) produced three independent UA batches (S1, S2, S3) of Mo–20Si–52.8Ti at.% alloy using a commercially available 3D Lab ATO system. More than 85% of particles fell in the 40–80 µm range across all three batches, with fewer than 6.4% below 40 µm and less than 0.2% below 20 µm (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031). The d90 values were 63, 72, and 78 µm for S1, S2, and S3, respectively — a range of 15 µm or approximately ±12% around the mean d90 of ~71 µm (pqac-00000031). No D10, D50, span, or formal standard deviations/CVs for the PSD percentiles were reported.

**For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run PSD statistics have been published.** The closest proxy is Yankin et al. (2025), who varied arc angle, current, and vibration amplitude for AlSi12 on a 3D Lab ATO (35 kHz). Across their seven deliberate parameter changes, D10 ranged from 38.7 to 44.7 µm (variation 13.5%), D50 from 52.3 to 54.7 µm (variation 4.4%), D90 from 66.4 to 72.7 µm (variation 8.7%), and span from 0.40 to 0.64 (variation 37.5%) (pqac-00000009). These represent parameter-sensitivity ranges, not replicate scatter; measurement standard deviations were not reported despite at least three laser-diffraction readings per sample (pqac-00000001).

For 316L stainless steel (recycled via PBF-LB), Bashmakova et al. (2026) atomized material under 18 combinations of current (70–160 A) and vibration amplitude (60–80%) at 35 kHz, with three rods per condition. Across conditions: d10 = 12–15 µm, d50 = 23–34 µm, d90 = 45–49 µm, and span = 1.00–1.46 (pqac-00000017). D90 was notably stable (range ≈4 µm) because the powder was sieved at the upper end, while d50 showed wider variation, and the span ranged from 1.00 to 1.46 depending on conditions. However, within-condition (rod-to-rod) statistics were not reported (pqac-00000020).

For Ti6Al4V, Bałasz et al. (2023) reported two UA batches with count-based PSD values of D10/D50/D90 = 40.2/52.0/60.8 and 41.2/51.4/63.4 µm, and span values of 0.37 and 0.43, respectively (pqac-00000007). The D50 values differed by ~1 µm, suggesting modest batch-to-batch variation, but with n = 2 and different underlying conditions, no statistical conclusion can be drawn.

For niobium, Wróbel et al. (2026) reported a single-batch PSD of D10/D50/D90 = 44.12/54.99/66.85 µm and span = 0.413 (pqac-00000004). No replicate data exist.

---

## (b) Spread in Yield

**No study reports replicate-run yield statistics (SD or CV) at fixed settings.** The available yield data vary considerably across alloys and equipment configurations, but always reflect parameter studies rather than replicate production runs:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** 45–50 wt.% of input rods converted to particles <100 µm, reported as a pooled range across three batches without batch-specific values (pqac-00000031).
- **AlSi12 (Yankin 2025):** Approximately 75% of the total powder passed a 63 µm sieve and was considered suitable for SLM (pqac-00000032).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Usable-powder yield ranged from 47% to 63% across the 18 process conditions. The highest yield (63%) was at minimum current (70 A) and lowest amplitude (60%). At amplitude-grouped averages: 59% at 60%, 53% at 70%, and 51% at 80% amplitude (pqac-00000015).
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** 94% of feed wire converted to powder <100 µm; 70.3% by mass in the 43–83 µm (63 ± 20 µm) range; after gas-flow optimization, >98% recovery was claimed (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).
- **Recycled Ti alloy (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder):** Over 85% of atomized powder was below 100 µm (pqac-00000043).

The yield variation across process conditions for 316L (47–63%, a range of 16 percentage points) provides the closest proxy for the sensitivity of yield to process perturbations (pqac-00000015).

---

## (c) Spread in Sphericity, Circularity, Aspect Ratio, and Satellite Fraction

**No published study reports run-to-run variability (SD or CV) for sphericity or satellite fraction.** The available data are:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** Greater than 90% of particles had aspect ratio <1.2 across all three batches, with particles described as satellite-free (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031). No batch-specific sphericity distributions were tabulated.
- **Nb (Wróbel 2026):** Mean sphericity 0.94; satellites, agglomerates, and oxidation defects were not observed (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Sphericity coefficient ranged from 0.84 to 0.90 across 18 process conditions, compared with 0.56 for virgin gas-atomized powder (pqac-00000006). The range of 0.06 across conditions is a proxy for process-induced shape variability.
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** Mean sphericity 0.88–0.90 for the two reported UA entries (pqac-00000007).
- **Sn–58Bi (Yang et al. 2026):** At the optimized condition (30% amplitude, 199 °C, Ar), sphericity = 0.87 and satellite index = 1.07. Sphericity decreased and satellite index increased with melt temperature (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).

---

## (d) Run-to-Run Variation in Composition and Oxygen Pickup

**The Hinrichs et al. (2021) Mo–Si–Ti dataset is the only published study with batch-specific oxygen measurements at fixed nominal UA settings.** The three batches yielded: S1 = 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 = 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm O, S3 = 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm O (pqac-00000031). Starting from a common as-cast oxygen content of ~460 ppm, the oxygen pickup during atomization was approximately 820–990 ppm per batch. The inter-batch mean is ~1353 ppm, with a batch-to-batch sample standard deviation of approximately 87 ppm and coefficient of variation of approximately 6.4%. ICP-OES analysis showed no significant changes in alloy composition (Mo, Si, Ti) across the three batches (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

For **316L stainless steel** (Bashmakova et al. 2026), the main alloying elements (Cr, Ni, Mo) remained within specification across the two extreme atomization conditions (70A/60% vs. 160A/80%). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).

# Run-to-Run Repeatability of Ultrasonic Atomization of Molten Metals: A Critical Review of Published Data

## Overview and Key Finding

**True fixed-setting, batch-to-batch replicate data for ultrasonic atomization (UA) of molten metals are extremely scarce in the open literature.** After a comprehensive search across journal publications and patents covering sonotrode/vibrating-plate UA systems (including AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO, and lab-built 20–60 kHz systems), only one study — Hinrichs et al. (2021) on Mo–20Si–52.8Ti — explicitly produced and compared multiple powder batches at nominally identical process settings to assess reproducibility. All other studies report single batches or parameter-variation campaigns that can only serve as proxies for process variability. No published data were found for true replicate runs on aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, Scalmalloy) or any other alloy system beyond the Mo-Si-Ti case. The following sections present what numerical data exist, organized by the requested categories.
