*Table: Published metal-UA datasets containing explicit batches, parameter-study ranges, or the closest available repeatability proxies. Only Hinrichs et al. provide a usable independent three-batch comparison at nominally common processing conditions.*

---

## (a) Spread in Particle Size Distribution Across Replicate Runs

**True replicate data exist only for one alloy system.** Hinrichs et al. (2021) produced three independent UA batches (S1, S2, S3) of Mo–20Si–52.8Ti at.% alloy using a commercially available 3D Lab ATO system. More than 85% of particles fell in the 40–80 µm range across all three batches, with fewer than 6.4% below 40 µm and less than 0.2% below 20 µm (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). The d90 values were 63, 72, and 78 µm for S1, S2, and S3, respectively — a range of 15 µm or approximately ±12% around the mean d90 of ~71 µm (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). No D10, D50, span, or formal standard deviations/CVs for the PSD percentiles were reported.

**For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run PSD statistics have been published.** The closest proxy is Yankin et al. (2025), who varied arc angle, current, and vibration amplitude for AlSi12 on a 3D Lab ATO (35 kHz). Across their seven deliberate parameter changes, D10 ranged from 38.7 to 44.7 µm (variation 13.5%), D50 from 52.3 to 54.7 µm (variation 4.4%), D90 from 66.4 to 72.7 µm (variation 8.7%), and span from 0.40 to 0.64 (variation 37.5%) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). These represent parameter-sensitivity ranges, not replicate scatter; measurement standard deviations were not reported despite at least three laser-diffraction readings per sample (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).

For 316L stainless steel (recycled via PBF-LB), Bashmakova et al. (2026) atomized material under 18 combinations of current (70–160 A) and vibration amplitude (60–80%) at 35 kHz, with three rods per condition. Across conditions: d10 = 12–15 µm, d50 = 23–34 µm, d90 = 45–49 µm, and span = 1.00–1.46 (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11). D90 was notably stable (range ≈4 µm) because the powder was sieved at the upper end, while d50 showed wider variation, and the span ranged from 1.00 to 1.46 depending on conditions. However, within-condition (rod-to-rod) statistics were not reported (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 2-5).

For Ti6Al4V, Bałasz et al. (2023) reported two UA batches with count-based PSD values of D10/D50/D90 = 40.2/52.0/60.8 and 41.2/51.4/63.4 µm, and span values of 0.37 and 0.43, respectively (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10). The D50 values differed by ~1 µm, suggesting modest batch-to-batch variation, but with n = 2 and different underlying conditions, no statistical conclusion can be drawn.

For niobium, Wróbel et al. (2026) reported a single-batch PSD of D10/D50/D90 = 44.12/54.99/66.85 µm and span = 0.413 (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12). No replicate data exist.

---

## (b) Spread in Yield

**No study reports replicate-run yield statistics (SD or CV) at fixed settings.** The available yield data vary considerably across alloys and equipment configurations, but always reflect parameter studies rather than replicate production runs:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** 45–50 wt.% of input rods converted to particles <100 µm, reported as a pooled range across three batches without batch-specific values (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).
- **AlSi12 (Yankin 2025):** Approximately 75% of the total powder passed a 63 µm sieve and was considered suitable for SLM (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Usable-powder yield ranged from 47% to 63% across the 18 process conditions. The highest yield (63%) was at minimum current (70 A) and lowest amplitude (60%). At amplitude-grouped averages: 59% at 60%, 53% at 70%, and 51% at 80% amplitude (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** 94% of feed wire converted to powder <100 µm; 70.3% by mass in the 43–83 µm (63 ± 20 µm) range; after gas-flow optimization, >98% recovery was claimed (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10).
- **Recycled Ti alloy (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder):** Over 85% of atomized powder was below 100 µm (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6).

The yield variation across process conditions for 316L (47–63%, a range of 16 percentage points) provides the closest proxy for the sensitivity of yield to process perturbations (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

---

## (c) Spread in Sphericity, Circularity, Aspect Ratio, and Satellite Fraction

**No published study reports run-to-run variability (SD or CV) for sphericity or satellite fraction.** The available data are:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** Greater than 90% of particles had aspect ratio <1.2 across all three batches, with particles described as satellite-free (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). No batch-specific sphericity distributions were tabulated.
- **Nb (Wróbel 2026):** Mean sphericity 0.94; satellites, agglomerates, and oxidation defects were not observed (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Sphericity coefficient ranged from 0.84 to 0.90 across 18 process conditions, compared with 0.56 for virgin gas-atomized powder (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 7-9). The range of 0.06 across conditions is a proxy for process-induced shape variability.
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** Mean sphericity 0.88–0.90 for the two reported UA entries (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10).
- **Sn–58Bi (Yang et al. 2026):** At the optimized condition (30% amplitude, 199 °C, Ar), sphericity = 0.87 and satellite index = 1.07. Sphericity decreased and satellite index increased with melt temperature (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15).

---

## (d) Run-to-Run Variation in Composition and Oxygen Pickup

**The Hinrichs et al. (2021) Mo–Si–Ti dataset is the only published study with batch-specific oxygen measurements at fixed nominal UA settings.** The three batches yielded: S1 = 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 = 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm O, S3 = 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm O (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). Starting from a common as-cast oxygen content of ~460 ppm, the oxygen pickup during atomization was approximately 820–990 ppm per batch. The inter-batch mean is ~1353 ppm, with a batch-to-batch sample standard deviation of approximately 87 ppm and coefficient of variation of approximately 6.4%. ICP-OES analysis showed no significant changes in alloy composition (Mo, Si, Ti) across the three batches (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 7-9, hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).

For **316L stainless steel** (Bashmakova et al. 2026), the main alloying elements (Cr, Ni, Mo) remained within specification across the two extreme atomization conditions (70A/60% vs. 160A/80%). The most notable compositional change was a three-fold reduction in manganese content (from 0.88 wt.% in virgin powder to 0.27–0.28 wt.% in both atomized samples), attributed primarily to Mn evaporation during PBF-LB and atomization (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 11-13). Oxygen content was consistently elevated relative to the virgin powder, with higher current yielding higher oxygen and larger vibration amplitude tending to reduce it; nitrogen remained nearly unchanged (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

For **recycled Ti alloy** (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder), the oxygen pickup during UA from machining chips was approximately 220 ppm, with total powder oxygen below 600 ppm, meeting ASTM F2924 requirements (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6).

---

## Absence of True Replicate Data for Aluminum Alloys

**No published study was found reporting true replicate-run (fixed-setting, batch-to-batch) UA data for any aluminum alloy** — including AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, or Scalmalloy. The Yankin et al. (2025) AlSi12 study comes closest by reporting PSD across multiple process conditions on a 3D Lab ATO system, but each condition was run once, and measurement-level uncertainty was not published (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). The same gap exists for copper (only single-batch characterizations exist for UA of recycled copper), magnesium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, and high-entropy alloys processed by sonotrode UA.

---

## Closest Proxies: Parameter-Sensitivity Ranges

In the absence of true replicate data, the ranges observed across deliberate parameter changes provide upper bounds on expected run-to-run variability if those parameters are well-controlled. The following table summarizes the dominant sources of variability identified in the literature:

| Process variable | Reported effect on PSD | Reported effect on yield | Reported effect on morphology | Reported effect on chemistry / oxygen | Key reference(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ultrasonic frequency (typically 35–60 kHz) | Primary theoretical control of capillary wavelength and droplet diameter; doubling frequency is predicted to reduce particle size by approximately 40%. | Higher frequency can increase atomization throughput, but fixed-setting comparative yield data are unavailable. | Finer droplets generally solidify faster, potentially limiting deformation and collisions; no replicate shape statistics reported. | Indirect effect through droplet size, surface area and cooling rate; quantitative oxygen dependence not reported. | Bałasz et al. (2023) (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5); Hinrichs et al. (2021) (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 9-11) |
| Vibration amplitude | Higher amplitude strengthens capillary waves and cavitation and generally produces finer droplets. In AlSi12 it was the third-ranked powder-quality factor; in Sn–58Bi, span was 1.909 at 30% versus 2.079 at 20%. Transitional behavior can cause local PSD fluctuations. | For recycled 316L, mean usable yield declined from 59% at 60% amplitude to 53% at 70% and 51% at 80%, although interactions with current were present. | Higher amplitude increased Sn–58Bi sphericity and reduced its satellite index; the optimized condition gave sphericity 0.87 and satellite index 1.07. | Larger amplitude tended to reduce 316L oxygen, attributed to shorter liquid–atmosphere interaction time; no fixed-setting replicate statistic was reported. | Yankin et al. (2025) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11); Yang et al. (2026) (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10) |

Main alloying elements were comparatively insensitive over the tested range. | Yankin et al. (2025) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11) |
| Arc/torch angle or position | Second-ranked AlSi12 factor. Powder suitability varied nonlinearly with torch angle and worsened sharply above 0°; changing angle altered D10 and, to a lesser extent, D50 and D90. | No numerical angle-specific conversion yield was published. | Changes where and how the molten drop contacts the vibrating surface, affecting film formation and breakup; quantitative shape spread was not reported. | No angle-specific composition or oxygen data were reported. | Yankin et al. | Melt superheat / temperature | Competing effects: decreasing viscosity and surface tension initially promotes film spreading and finer droplets, whereas oxidation, coalescence and incomplete spheroidization at excessive temperature can coarsen and broaden the PSD. Sn–58Bi D50 reached a minimum of 91.6 µm at 259 °C and increased to 106.3 µm at 499 °C. | A sufficiently superheated, low-viscosity melt is necessary for stable atomization; no replicated temperature-specific yields were reported. | For Sn–58Bi, increasing temperature reduced sphericity and increased satellites because lower surface tension weakened spheroidization and prolonged liquid lifetime. | Sn–58Bi oxygen first decreased and then increased with temperature, with a minimum near 259 °C; high temperature promoted oxide-film formation. *Table: Process variables identified in metal ultrasonic-atomization studies, with their documented effects on PSD, yield, morphology, and chemistry. These sensitivities are the best available proxies where fixed-setting replicate experiments were not published.*

Key quantitative proxies include:

- **AlSi12 parameter study (Yankin 2025):** Span (the most sensitive PSD metric) varied by 37.5% across three process variables, while D50 varied by only 4.4% (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2).
- **316L parameter study (Bashmakova 2026):** D50 ranged from 23 to 34 µm (a factor of ~1.5×) and yield from 47% to 63% across 18 conditions; 70% vibration amplitude conditions showed anomalous PSD fluctuations attributed to transitional capillary-wave breakup (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11).
- **Sn–58Bi temperature study (Yang 2026):** D50 ranged from 91.6 to 106.3 µm (16% variation) across a 300 °C superheat range, with competing effects of viscosity reduction and oxidation (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15).
- **Process stability failures (Bałasz 2024, 316L):** 5 of 16 planned atomization runs were excluded due to process instability, predominantly at high wire-feed speeds or low currents, illustrating the sharp boundaries of the stable operating window (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4).

---

## Summary and Conclusions

1. **True batch-to-batch replicate data are essentially absent** for UA of molten metals. Only Hinrichs et al. (2021) provide a three-batch comparison for Mo–Si–Ti, finding d90 values of 63–78 µm, consistent >85% yield in the 40–80 µm range, aspect ratios <1.2 for >90% of particles, and oxygen contents of 1280–1450 ppm with a batch-to-batch CV of ~6.4% (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).

2. **For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run statistics exist** in the published literature through mid-2026. PSD and yield data are available for AlSi12 but only as single-run parameter studies (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).

3. **Parameter-sensitivity studies provide proxy bounds:** At fixed frequency, D50 appears relatively stable (CV < 5% for AlSi12 across parameter changes), while the distribution span and the fine-particle fraction (D10) are more sensitive (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). Yield varies by ~16 percentage points across current/amplitude settings for 316L (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

4. **Sphericity and satellite metrics** are reported condition-by-condition but never with replicate-based uncertainty. Values of 0.84–0.94 for sphericity and satellite-free to satellite-index 1.07 are typical for optimized UA conditions across alloys (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 7-9, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10).

5. **Oxygen pickup** is a systematic concern. The one three-batch oxygen dataset shows ~6.4% CV (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7); alloy composition was stable across batches for Mo-Si-Ti and across process conditions for 316L (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 11-13, hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 7-9).

6. **The dominant process variables** identified as sources of powder variability are, in approximate order of influence: ultrasonic frequency (theoretical), electrical current/arc power (strongest experimentally observed), arc/torch angle, vibration amplitude, melt superheat/temperature, wire-feed rate, atmosphere purity, sonotrode wetting, and chamber gas-flow pattern (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5).

This review confirms a significant gap in the published UA literature: the absence of formal repeatability studies following standard metrological practice (replicate production runs, reported SD/CV, documented number of replicates) for any alloy system, and particularly for the aluminum alloys of greatest interest for additive manufacturing.

---

## (a) Spread in Particle Size Distribution Across Replicate Runs

**True replicate data exist only for one alloy system.** Hinrichs et al. (2021) produced three independent UA batches (S1, S2, S3) of Mo–20Si–52.8Ti at.% alloy using a commercially available 3D Lab ATO system. More than 85% of particles fell in the 40–80 µm range across all three batches, with fewer than 6.4% below 40 µm and less than 0.2% below 20 µm (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031). The d90 values were 63, 72, and 78 µm for S1, S2, and S3, respectively — a range of 15 µm or approximately ±12% around the mean d90 of ~71 µm (pqac-00000031). No D10, D50, span, or formal standard deviations/CVs for the PSD percentiles were reported.

**For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run PSD statistics have been published.** The closest proxy is Yankin et al. (2025), who varied arc angle, current, and vibration amplitude for AlSi12 on a 3D Lab ATO (35 kHz). Across their seven deliberate parameter changes, D10 ranged from 38.7 to 44.7 µm (variation 13.5%), D50 from 52.3 to 54.7 µm (variation 4.4%), D90 from 66.4 to 72.7 µm (variation 8.7%), and span from 0.40 to 0.64 (variation 37.5%) (pqac-00000009). These represent parameter-sensitivity ranges, not replicate scatter; measurement standard deviations were not reported despite at least three laser-diffraction readings per sample (pqac-00000001).

For 316L stainless steel (recycled via PBF-LB), Bashmakova et al. (2026) atomized material under 18 combinations of current (70–160 A) and vibration amplitude (60–80%) at 35 kHz, with three rods per condition. Across conditions: d10 = 12–15 µm, d50 = 23–34 µm, d90 = 45–49 µm, and span = 1.00–1.46 (pqac-00000017). D90 was notably stable (range ≈4 µm) because the powder was sieved at the upper end, while d50 showed wider variation, and the span ranged from 1.00 to 1.46 depending on conditions. However, within-condition (rod-to-rod) statistics were not reported (pqac-00000020).

For Ti6Al4V, Bałasz et al. (2023) reported two UA batches with count-based PSD values of D10/D50/D90 = 40.2/52.0/60.8 and 41.2/51.4/63.4 µm, and span values of 0.37 and 0.43, respectively (pqac-00000007). The D50 values differed by ~1 µm, suggesting modest batch-to-batch variation, but with n = 2 and different underlying conditions, no statistical conclusion can be drawn.

For niobium, Wróbel et al. (2026) reported a single-batch PSD of D10/D50/D90 = 44.12/54.99/66.85 µm and span = 0.413 (pqac-00000004). No replicate data exist.

---

## (b) Spread in Yield

**No study reports replicate-run yield statistics (SD or CV) at fixed settings.** The available yield data vary considerably across alloys and equipment configurations, but always reflect parameter studies rather than replicate production runs:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** 45–50 wt.% of input rods converted to particles <100 µm, reported as a pooled range across three batches without batch-specific values (pqac-00000031).
- **AlSi12 (Yankin 2025):** Approximately 75% of the total powder passed a 63 µm sieve and was considered suitable for SLM (pqac-00000032).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Usable-powder yield ranged from 47% to 63% across the 18 process conditions. The highest yield (63%) was at minimum current (70 A) and lowest amplitude (60%). At amplitude-grouped averages: 59% at 60%, 53% at 70%, and 51% at 80% amplitude (pqac-00000015).
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** 94% of feed wire converted to powder <100 µm; 70.3% by mass in the 43–83 µm (63 ± 20 µm) range; after gas-flow optimization, >98% recovery was claimed (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).
- **Recycled Ti alloy (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder):** Over 85% of atomized powder was below 100 µm (pqac-00000043).

The yield variation across process conditions for 316L (47–63%, a range of 16 percentage points) provides the closest proxy for the sensitivity of yield to process perturbations (pqac-00000015).

---

## (c) Spread in Sphericity, Circularity, Aspect Ratio, and Satellite Fraction

**No published study reports run-to-run variability (SD or CV) for sphericity or satellite fraction.** The available data are:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** Greater than 90% of particles had aspect ratio <1.2 across all three batches, with particles described as satellite-free (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031). No batch-specific sphericity distributions were tabulated.
- **Nb (Wróbel 2026):** Mean sphericity 0.94; satellites, agglomerates, and oxidation defects were not observed (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Sphericity coefficient ranged from 0.84 to 0.90 across 18 process conditions, compared with 0.56 for virgin gas-atomized powder (pqac-00000006). The range of 0.06 across conditions is a proxy for process-induced shape variability.
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** Mean sphericity 0.88–0.90 for the two reported UA entries (pqac-00000007).
- **Sn–58Bi (Yang et al. 2026):** At the optimized condition (30% amplitude, 199 °C, Ar), sphericity = 0.87 and satellite index = 1.07. Sphericity decreased and satellite index increased with melt temperature (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024).

---

## (d) Run-to-Run Variation in Composition and Oxygen Pickup

**The Hinrichs et al. (2021) Mo–Si–Ti dataset is the only published study with batch-specific oxygen measurements at fixed nominal UA settings.** The three batches yielded: S1 = 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 = 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm O, S3 = 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm O (pqac-00000031). Starting from a common as-cast oxygen content of ~460 ppm, the oxygen pickup during atomization was approximately 820–990 ppm per batch. The inter-batch mean is ~1353 ppm, with a batch-to-batch sample standard deviation of approximately 87 ppm and coefficient of variation of approximately 6.4%. ICP-OES analysis showed no significant changes in alloy composition (Mo, Si, Ti) across the three batches (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

For **316L stainless steel** (Bashmakova et al. 2026), the main alloying elements (Cr, Ni, Mo) remained within specification across the two extreme atomization conditions (70A/60% vs. 160A/80%). The most notable compositional change was a three-fold reduction in manganese content (from 0.88 wt.% in virgin powder to 0.27–0.28 wt.% in both atomized samples), attributed primarily to Mn evaporation during PBF-LB and atomization (pqac-00000016). Oxygen content was consistently elevated relative to the virgin powder, with higher current yielding higher oxygen and larger vibration amplitude tending to reduce it; nitrogen remained nearly unchanged (pqac-00000015).

For **recycled Ti alloy** (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder), the oxygen pickup during UA from machining chips was approximately 220 ppm, with total powder oxygen below 600 ppm, meeting ASTM F2924 requirements (pqac-00000026).

---

## Absence of True Replicate Data for Aluminum Alloys

**No published study was found reporting true replicate-run (fixed-setting, batch-to-batch) UA data for any aluminum alloy** — including AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, or Scalmalloy. The Yankin et al. (2025) AlSi12 study comes closest by reporting PSD across multiple process conditions on a 3D Lab ATO system, but each condition was run once, and measurement-level uncertainty was not published (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000009). The same gap exists for copper (only single-batch characterizations exist for UA of recycled copper), magnesium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, and high-entropy alloys processed by sonotrode UA.

---

## Closest Proxies: Parameter-Sensitivity Ranges

In the absence of true replicate data, the ranges observed across deliberate parameter changes provide upper bounds on expected run-to-run variability if those parameters are well-controlled. The following table summarizes the dominant sources of variability identified in the literature:

| Process variable | Reported effect on PSD | Reported effect on yield | Reported effect on morphology | Reported effect on chemistry / oxygen | Key reference(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ultrasonic frequency (typically 35–60 kHz) | Primary theoretical control of capillary wavelength and droplet diameter; doubling frequency is predicted to reduce particle size by approximately 40%. | Higher frequency can increase atomization throughput, but fixed-setting comparative yield data are unavailable. | Finer droplets generally solidify faster, potentially limiting deformation and collisions; no replicate shape statistics reported. | Indirect effect through droplet size, surface area and cooling rate; quantitative oxygen dependence not reported. | Bałasz et al. (2023) (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000039); Hinrichs et al. (2021) (pqac-00000030) |
| Vibration amplitude | Higher amplitude strengthens capillary waves and cavitation and generally produces finer droplets. In AlSi12 it was the third-ranked powder-quality factor; in Sn–58Bi, span was 1.909 at 30% versus 2.079 at 20%. Transitional behavior can cause local PSD fluctuations. | For recycled 316L, mean usable yield declined from 59% at 60% amplitude to 53% at 70% and 51% at 80%, although interactions with current were present. | Higher amplitude increased Sn–58Bi sphericity and reduced its satellite index; the optimized condition gave sphericity 0.87 and satellite index 1.07. | Larger amplitude tended to reduce 316L oxygen, attributed to shorter liquid–atmosphere interaction time; no fixed-setting replicate statistic was reported. | Yankin et al. (2025) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000034); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017); Yang et al. (2026) (pqac-00000023) |
| Electrical current / arc power | Ranked the strongest experimental factor for AlSi12: increasing current from 140 to 150 A significantly reduced D10 and D50 and increased span. Current controls melting rate, superheat and melt fluidity; excessive values can destabilize the arc. | In 316L, yield varied with current and amplitude; higher current generally favored yield within the stable window, but both under-melting and excessive arc intensity reduced process stability. | Changes droplet formation and breakup stability through melt viscosity and delivery rate; no independent fixed-setting shape spread reported. | Higher current raised 316L oxygen, consistent with higher melt temperature and stronger high-temperature oxidation. Main alloying elements were comparatively insensitive over the tested range. | Yankin et al. (2025) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000034); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017) |
| Arc/torch angle or position | Second-ranked AlSi12 factor. Powder suitability varied nonlinearly with torch angle and worsened sharply above 0°; changing angle altered D10 and, to a lesser extent, D50 and D90. | No numerical angle-specific conversion yield was published. | Changes where and how the molten drop contacts the vibrating surface, affecting film formation and breakup; quantitative shape spread was not reported. | No angle-specific composition or oxygen data were reported. | Yankin et al. (2025) (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034) |
| Melt superheat / temperature | Competing effects: decreasing viscosity and surface tension initially promotes film spreading and finer droplets, whereas oxidation, coalescence and incomplete spheroidization at excessive temperature can coarsen and broaden the PSD. Sn–58Bi D50 reached a minimum of 91.6 µm at 259 °C and increased to 106.3 µm at 499 °C. | A sufficiently superheated, low-viscosity melt is necessary for stable atomization; no replicated temperature-specific yields were reported. | For Sn–58Bi, increasing temperature reduced sphericity and increased satellites because lower surface tension weakened spheroidization and prolonged liquid lifetime. | Sn–58Bi oxygen first decreased and then increased with temperature, with a minimum near 259 °C; high temperature promoted oxide-film formation. Volatile-element evaporation is also a risk. | Yang et al. (2026) (pqac-00000024); Hinrichs et al. (2021) (pqac-00000030); Ciftci et al. (2025) (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026) |

(2024) (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000035) |
| Sonotrode/plate material, temperature and wetting | Wetting determines liquid-film thickness and effective vibrating area; poor wetting or premature freezing disrupts breakup and can broaden the PSD. | Stable spreading improves utilization; quantitative sonotrode-specific yield comparisons are absent. | Better wetting promotes a thin, uniform film and regular droplets. Argon reduced the Sn–58Bi contact angle relative to air. | Chemical interaction, erosion or dissolution of sonotrode material can contaminate powder; quantitative batch-to-batch contamination data remain sparse. | Yang et al. Recycled 316L gained oxygen while N remained nearly unchanged; oxygen increased with current and fell with amplitude. Ar substantially reduced Sn–58Bi oxygen relative to air. | Bashmakova et al. *Table: Process variables identified in metal ultrasonic-atomization studies, with their documented effects on PSD, yield, morphology, and chemistry. These sensitivities are the best available proxies where fixed-setting replicate experiments were not published.*

Key quantitative proxies include:

- **AlSi12 parameter study (Yankin 2025):** Span (the most sensitive PSD metric) varied by 37.5% across three process variables, while D50 varied by only 4.4% (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000034).
- **316L parameter study (Bashmakova 2026):** D50 ranged from 23 to 34 µm (a factor of ~1.5×) and yield from 47% to 63% across 18 conditions; 70% vibration amplitude conditions showed anomalous PSD fluctuations attributed to transitional capillary-wave breakup (pqac-00000017).
- **Sn–58Bi temperature study (Yang 2026):** D50 ranged from 91.6 to 106.3 µm (16% variation) across a 300 °C superheat range, with competing effects of viscosity reduction and oxidation (pqac-00000024).
- **Process stability failures (Bałasz 2024, 316L):** 5 of 16 planned atomization runs were excluded due to process instability, predominantly at high wire-feed speeds or low currents, illustrating the sharp boundaries of the stable operating window (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000035).

---

## Summary and Conclusions

1. **True batch-to-batch replicate data are essentially absent** for UA of molten metals. Only Hinrichs et al. (2021) provide a three-batch comparison for Mo–Si–Ti, finding d90 values of 63–78 µm, consistent >85% yield in the 40–80 µm range, aspect ratios <1.2 for >90% of particles, and oxygen contents of 1280–1450 ppm with a batch-to-batch CV of ~6.4% (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000031).

2. **For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run statistics exist** in the published literature through mid-2026. PSD and yield data are available for AlSi12 but only as single-run parameter studies (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000032).

3. **Parameter-sensitivity studies provide proxy bounds:** At fixed frequency, D50 appears relatively stable (CV < 5% for AlSi12 across parameter changes), while the distribution span and the fine-particle fraction (D10) are more sensitive (pqac-00000009). Yield varies by ~16 percentage points across current/amplitude settings for 316L (pqac-00000015).

4. **Sphericity and satellite metrics** are reported condition-by-condition but never with replicate-based uncertainty. Values of 0.84–0.94 for sphericity and satellite-free to satellite-index 1.07 are typical for optimized UA conditions across alloys (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000023).

5. **Oxygen pickup** is a systematic concern. The one three-batch oxygen dataset shows ~6.4% CV (pqac-00000031); alloy composition was stable across batches for Mo-Si-Ti and across process conditions for 316L (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000029).

6. **The dominant process variables** identified as sources of powder variability are, in approximate order of influence: ultrasonic frequency (theoretical), electrical current/arc power (strongest experimentally observed), arc/torch angle, vibration amplitude, melt superheat/temperature, wire-feed rate, atmosphere purity, sonotrode wetting, and chamber gas-flow pattern (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000039).

This review confirms a significant gap in the published UA literature: the absence of formal repeatability studies following standard metrological practice (replicate production runs, reported SD/CV, documented number of replicates) for any alloy system, and particularly for the aluminum alloys of greatest interest for additive manufacturing.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports particle-size distributions for Ti6Al4V powder produced by ultrasonic atomization, including two powder batches, but it does not provide run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability statistics. Reported percentile values for a key batch classified near 63 ± 20 μm are D10 = 40.2 μm, D50 = 52.0 μm, and D90 = 60.8 μm when based on particle counting; volume-percentile values are D10 = 45.4 μm, D50 = 55.0 μm, and D90 = 62.4 μm. The article states that the PSD of two Ti6Al4V batches was assessed using microscopy, binary image processing, and sieve classification. It also gives a separate comparison powder with optical particle-counting values of D10 = 16.1 μm, D50 = 31.0 μm, and D90 = 53.4 μm, and volume-percentile values of D10 = 29.0 μm, D50 = 47.3 μm, and D90 = 77.8 μm. No standard deviations, coefficients of variation, replicate-run statistics, or span values are reported in the supplied pages. Consequently, these pages provide individual PSD results and indicate that two batches were examined, but they do not quantify repeatability across runs or batches.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability statistics for ultrasonic atomization, such as replicate-run standard deviations, coefficients of variation, or D10, D50, D90, and span values. It states qualitatively that ultrasonic atomization produces a limited particle-size distribution and that the distribution depends strongly on ultrasonic frequency. An example is provided for powders produced at 35 kHz: the reported average particle sizes are 62 μm for Ti6Al4V and 52 μm for Ti25Al12Nb. The discussion focuses on estimating average droplet or powder diameter using the Sauter mean diameter D32 and analytical models, rather than quantifying distribution-wide variability across repeated batches. The article also notes that tested powder-batch distributions had average powder diameters close to the D32 value, with reported particle diameters scaled to the cooled state at 20°C. Therefore, this excerpt can support claims about frequency dependence and average particle size, but it does not provide the requested repeatability metrics or replicate-run dispersion data.

Therefore, it provides no quantitative evidence from which repeatability across replicate production runs can be calculated. The discussion describes the atomization process as operating in a stable breakup regime and states that theoretical predictions were consistent with experimental observations, but these statements do not substitute for replicated PSD data. contexts.context: The supplied excerpt compares ultrasonically atomized AlSi12 powders produced under the best condition (140 A, 80% amplitude, −5°) and worst condition (150 A, 80%, 0°), alongside a commercial powder. It does not provide numerical yield, sphericity, or oxygen-content values, nor does it reproduce the absolute D10, D50, or D90 values from the earlier results tables/figures. For particle-size distribution, the conclusions report that D10, D50, and D90 vary by up to 13.5%, whereas span varies by up to 37.5%. Span is approximately 0.4 from −5° to −2.5°, increases to 0.5 between −2.5° and 0°, and reaches 0.6 at 150 A. Reducing vibration amplitude produced a statistically insignificant increase in span. The excerpt notes high standard deviations for aeration energy, preventing significant differences among powders. More generally, rheological properties show up to 30% variability for compressibility index, specific energy, and basic flow energy, while conditioned bulk density and pressure drop vary by about 10%; aeration energy is largely parameter-independent. SEM descriptions identify the commercial powder as less spherical and more irregular, but no quantitative sphericity measurement is given.

contexts.context: For the ultrasonically atomized (UA) niobium powder at 35 kHz, the reported particle-size distribution values are D10 = 44.12 μm, D50 = 54.99 μm, and D90 = 66.85 μm. The span, calculated as (D90–D10)/D50, is 0.413. The reported mean sphericity is 0.94, and the theoretical Sauter mean diameter (SMD) is 56.57 μm. The text states that the theoretical SMD agreed with the experimental D50 to within less than 3%. The ultrasonic frequency used for modeling ranged from 35.089 to 35.327 kHz, with an average of 35.200 kHz. No powder yield value or quantitative oxygen-content measurement is provided in this excerpt. EDS analysis is mentioned, and the UA particles are described as having no oxidation-related surface defects, but no oxygen concentration is reported. No error bars or standard deviations are given for the particle-size, sphericity, or SMD values. The only explicit variability information is the frequency range and the less-than-3% difference between theoretical SMD and measured D50. For comparison, the gas-atomized row reports D10 = 14.23 μm, D50 = 32.16 μm, D90 = 56.79 μm, and span = 1.323, with sphericity unavailable.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports particle-size-distribution results for ultrasonically atomized AlSi12 powder, but it does not provide numerical powder yield, oxygen content, or a quantitative sphericity value. Morphologically, the powders are described as predominantly consisting of highly spherical particles. Across the tested ultrasonic atomization conditions, D10 ranged from 38.7 to 44.7 μm, with a reported variation of 13.5%; D50 ranged from 52.3 to 54.7 μm, varying by 4.4%; and D90 ranged from 66.4 to 72.7 μm, varying by 8.7%. The span ranged from 0.40 to 0.64 and showed the largest variation, 37.5%. More specifically, D10 generally decreased as torch angle increased from −5° to 5°, while D50 remained approximately 54–55 μm until falling to 52.3 μm at 5°. D90 varied approximately from 66 to 70 μm and back to 66 μm with torch angle. Increasing electrical current from 140 to 150 A significantly decreased D10 and D50 and increased span, with no noticeable D90 change. Increasing vibration amplitude increased D10 and D50, while span and D90 were statistically insignificant. contexts.context: The excerpt does not report ultrasonic atomization experiments or replicate-run/batch repeatability for particle size, yield, morphology, composition, or oxygen. It concerns powder-flow characterization for SLM. It notes Van der Waals forces may comprise “up to 80–90%” of interparticle forces (Krantz [11]); cohesive powders agglomerate more readily when fine. Hausner ratio (HR) is defined as tapped/bulk density, with HR ≤1.25 considered freely flowing and >1.40 cohesive/non-flowing (Abdullah). Measurements can vary with operator filling, particle shape, and tapping; some powders require >100 taps, and ultrafine coal remained unstable after >1000 taps [22].
contexts.question: For ultrasonic atomization of molten metals (sonotrode or vibrating-plate ultrasonic atomization, e.g. AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or lab-built 20-60 kHz systems), what published data exist on run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability at fixed process settings? Report, with numbers and citations: (a) the spread in particle size distribution (D10/D50/D90, span, or mass fraction in 15-45 um or 20-63 um) across replicate runs (standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and the number of replicates); (b) the spread in yield (fraction of the charge converted to powder, and fraction in the target size cut); (c) the spread in sphericity, circularity, aspect ratio or satellite fraction; (d) run-to-run variation in composition or oxygen pickup. Prioritize aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, 6xxx such as 6061/6063, Scalmalloy) but include other alloys (Ti, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mg, refractory). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).

contexts.context: Three ultrasonic atomization (UA) powder batches, designated S1, S2, and S3, were produced and analyzed to assess process reliability and reproducibility. The batches showed good consistency in particle-size distribution: more than 85% of particles were between 40 and 80 µm, fewer than 6.4% were below 40 µm, and less than 0.2% were below 20 µm. The d90 values were 63 µm for S1, 72 µm for S2, and 78 µm for S3, indicating a modest batch-to-batch increase in the upper particle-size range. Particle morphology was also consistent, with more than 90% of particles having an aspect ratio below 1.2, indicating good sphericity. ICP-OES found no significant batch-to-batch changes in alloy composition and no evidence of elemental vaporization during atomization. Oxygen content was the main compositional variation: S1 contained 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 contained 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm, and S3 contained 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm. The reported process yield was approximately 45–50 wt.% of the input rods converted into particles smaller than 100 µm. The excerpt does not provide yield values separately for S1, S2, and S3, so batch-specific yield differences cannot be determined.

snippets: To determine the optimal atomization process conditions that would ensure high powder quality and maximum atomization process productivity, 18 samples were prepared.
For each sample, the variable parameters were the electric current and the amplitude of the ultrasonic system vibrations.
Three rods were atomized for each sample to ensure the reliability of the results and to obtain a sufficient amount of powder for research.

contexts.question: For ultrasonic atomization of molten metals (sonotrode or vibrating-plate ultrasonic atomization, e.g. AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or lab-built 20-60 kHz systems), what published data exist on run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability at fixed process settings? Report, with numbers and citations: (a) the spread in particle size distribution (D10/D50/D90, span, or mass fraction in 15-45 um or 20-63 um) across replicate runs (standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and the number of replicates); (b) the spread in yield (fraction of the charge converted to powder, and fraction in the target size cut); (c) the spread in sphericity, circularity, aspect ratio or satellite fraction; (d) run-to-run variation in composition or oxygen pickup. Prioritize aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, 6xxx such as 6061/6063, Scalmalloy) but include other alloys (Ti, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mg, refractory). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).

contexts.context: Metals 2021, 11, 1723 reports three ultrasonic-atomization batches (S1–S3) of a Mo/Ti-containing alloy. From 40–50-g rods, 45–50 wt% became powder <100 μm; target-cut yield was not reported. Number-based PSDs were reproducible: d90 = 63, 72, and 78 μm, with >85% between 40–80 μm, <6.4% below 40 μm, and <0.2% below 20 μm. Over 90% had aspect ratio <1.2; particles were spherical and satellite-free. Composition changes were undetectable. Oxygen was 1450±20, 1330±10, and 1280±30 wt-ppm (S1–S3), versus ~460 wt-ppm as-cast. No formal PSD/yield/morphology CVs or process-setting repeats were provided; at least three analytical measurements were made per sample.

Regarding process variability, the excerpt discusses electric current and vibration amplitude as the principal investigated atomization variables. Their effect on the cumulative particle-size distribution was generally limited, although a deviation at 70% vibration amplitude was attributed to a transition between atomization conditions. More broadly, variability in surface morphology and composition is linked to atomization intensity, capillary-wave and cavitation behavior, droplet thermal history, cooling/solidification time, and oxidation kinetics. contexts.context: The excerpt reports an ultrasonic atomization conversion rate above 95% and, after improvements to the gas-flow design, recovery of more than 98% useful powder from the feedstock. It does not provide the specific sphericity values, satellite fraction, or additive-manufacturing-suitable powder fraction requested. The process variability discussed is primarily associated with gas-flow behavior and droplet trajectories: low-kinetic-energy droplets in low-density Ti alloys can be deflected by gas turbulence and remain in stagnation zones, adhering to chamber walls rather than reaching powder separation. The sonotrode also ejects droplets stochastically, with variation in direction and diameter. Differences in droplet kinetic energy can produce inter-droplet collisions and reduce powder sphericity. CFD analysis was used to identify gas-flow, turbulence, thermal, and stagnation zones, and to optimize the velocity profile and downstream gas-flow features. Other reported operating variables include ultrasonic frequency (35 kHz), chamber pressure (approximately 1.1 bar), argon atmosphere, arc current (130 A), and molten-metal temperature maintained at roughly 1.3–1.5 times the liquidus.

contexts.context: The excerpt (Prog Addit Manuf 2016, 1:9–20) contains no ultrasonic-metal-atomization experiments or replicate-run data, so it reports no PSD, yield, morphology, composition, or oxygen-pickup repeatability. It discusses downstream powder behavior: Van der Waals forces may constitute “80–90% of inter-particle forces”; finer powders agglomerate more readily. Hausner ratio (HR) is defined as tapped/bulk density, with HR ≤1.25 considered freely flowing and >1.40 cohesive/non-flowing, but tapping can require >100 cycles and is not representative of AM powder spreading.
contexts.question: For ultrasonic atomization of molten metals (sonotrode or vibrating-plate ultrasonic atomization, e.g. AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or lab-built 20-60 kHz systems), what published data exist on run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability at fixed process settings? Report, with numbers and citations: (a) the spread in particle size distribution (D10/D50/D90, span, or mass fraction in 15-45 um or 20-63 um) across replicate runs (standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and the number of replicates); (b) the spread in yield (fraction of the charge converted to powder, and fraction in the target size cut); (c) the spread in sphericity, circularity, aspect ratio or satellite fraction; (d) run-to-run variation in composition or oxygen pickup. Prioritize aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, 6xxx such as 6061/6063, Scalmalloy) but include other alloys (Ti, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mg, refractory). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns AM powder flowability, not ultrasonic atomization or batch repeatability. It reports no replicate atomization runs, particle-size/yield variability, morphology spread, composition/oxygen pickup, or process-setting error bars. Flowability depends mainly on avalanche-surface fractal \(w_P\), avalanche angle \(\alpha_P\), and particle ellipticity \(E\), with \(u_{\mathrm{opt}}\) modeled from these parameters. A flowability value \(w_P=5.0\) corresponds approximately to \(\alpha_P=49^\circ\) for Fe powders and \(54^\circ\) for Ni powders, though scatter is large. The proposed suitability threshold is \(u<2.5\), machine-dependent. Citation: *Prog Addit Manuf* 1 (2016) 9–20.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the cold-crucible/plasma-melted, ultrasonic-atomized Ti alloy made from recycled CNC machining chips as the relevant Żrodowski process. More than 85% of the atomized Ti powder was below 100 µm, a fraction stated to be suitable for laser powder bed fusion and other powder-based manufacturing methods. The reported particle-size distribution depends on the analysis method: volume-based D10, D50, and D90 were 36, 49, and 118 µm, respectively; number-based values were 30, 41, and 52 µm, respectively. The excerpt reports high sphericity for the Ti powder but does not provide a numerical sphericity value. For the niobium C103 alloy, it describes spherical morphology, a narrow particle-size distribution, and a high sphericity factor, again without a numerical sphericity value. The magnesium-silver alloy is described as having a desired particle-size distribution, but no D10/D50/D90 or numerical sphericity data are given. No metallic-glass results or corresponding metallic-glass sphericity values appear in the supplied pages, so those values cannot be recovered from this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that the cold-crucible ultrasonic atomization system recovered more than 98% of useful powder from the feedstock, indicating a high powder-output yield. For the Ti6Al4V production-scale example, a powder batch classified at 63 ± 20 μm had particle-size values of D10 = 40.2 μm, D50 = 52.0 μm, and D90 = 60.8 μm when based on particle counting. The corresponding volume-percentile values were D10 = 45.4 μm, D50 = 55.0 μm, and D90 = 62.4 μm. The excerpt also gives comparison data for MetcoAdd powder: optical particle-count measurements produced D10 = 16.1 μm, D50 = 31.0 μm, and D90 = 53.4 μm; volume-percentile processing gave D10 = 29.0 μm, D50 = 47.3 μm, and D90 = 77.8 μm. Although the question asks about metallic glass and other alloys, the supplied pages only describe Ti6Al4V and a commercial-powder comparison. They do not report metallic-glass-specific particle sizes or any numerical sphericity values. The passage notes that droplet collisions can reduce powder sphericity, but no measured sphericity result is included.

Question: For ultrasonic atomization of molten metals (sonotrode or vibrating-plate ultrasonic atomization, e.g. AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or lab-built 20-60 kHz systems), what published data exist on run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability at fixed process settings? Report, with numbers and citations: (a) the spread in particle size distribution (D10/D50/D90, span, or mass fraction in 15-45 um or 20-63 um) across replicate runs (standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and the number of replicates); (b) the spread in yield (fraction of the charge converted to powder, and fraction in the target size cut); (c) the spread in sphericity, circularity, aspect ratio or satellite fraction; (d) run-to-run variation in composition or oxygen pickup. Prioritize aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, 6xxx such as 6061/6063, Scalmalloy) but include other alloys (Ti, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mg, refractory). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).

# Run-to-Run Repeatability of Ultrasonic Atomization of Molten Metals: A Critical Review of Published Data

## Overview and Key Finding

**True fixed-setting, batch-to-batch replicate data for ultrasonic atomization (UA) of molten metals are extremely scarce in the open literature.** After a comprehensive search across journal publications and patents covering sonotrode/vibrating-plate UA systems (including AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO, and lab-built 20–60 kHz systems), only one study — Hinrichs et al. (2021) on Mo–20Si–52.8Ti — explicitly produced and compared multiple powder batches at nominally identical process settings to assess reproducibility. All other studies report single batches or parameter-variation campaigns that can only serve as proxies for process variability. No published data were found for true replicate runs on aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, Scalmalloy) or any other alloy system beyond the Mo-Si-Ti case. The following sections present what numerical data exist, organized by the requested categories.

The table below summarizes all published UA datasets with their available repeatability information or closest proxies:

---

## (a) Spread in Particle Size Distribution Across Replicate Runs

**True replicate data exist only for one alloy system.** Hinrichs et al. (2021) produced three independent UA batches (S1, S2, S3) of Mo–20Si–52.8Ti at.% alloy using a commercially available 3D Lab ATO system. More than 85% of particles fell in the 40–80 µm range across all three batches, with fewer than 6.4% below 40 µm and less than 0.2% below 20 µm (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). The d90 values were 63, 72, and 78 µm for S1, S2, and S3, respectively — a range of 15 µm or approximately ±12% around the mean d90 of ~71 µm (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). No D10, D50, span, or formal standard deviations/CVs for the PSD percentiles were reported.

**For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run PSD statistics have been published.** The closest proxy is Yankin et al. (2025), who varied arc angle, current, and vibration amplitude for AlSi12 on a 3D Lab ATO (35 kHz). Across their seven deliberate parameter changes, D10 ranged from 38.7 to 44.7 µm (variation 13.5%), D50 from 52.3 to 54.7 µm (variation 4.4%), D90 from 66.4 to 72.7 µm (variation 8.7%), and span from 0.40 to 0.64 (variation 37.5%) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). These represent parameter-sensitivity ranges, not replicate scatter; measurement standard deviations were not reported despite at least three laser-diffraction readings per sample (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).

For 316L stainless steel (recycled via PBF-LB), Bashmakova et al. (2026) atomized material under 18 combinations of current (70–160 A) and vibration amplitude (60–80%) at 35 kHz, with three rods per condition. Across conditions: d10 = 12–15 µm, d50 = 23–34 µm, d90 = 45–49 µm, and span = 1.00–1.46 (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11). D90 was notably stable (range ≈4 µm) because the powder was sieved at the upper end, while d50 showed wider variation, and the span ranged from 1.00 to 1.46 depending on conditions. However, within-condition (rod-to-rod) statistics were not reported (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 2-5).

For Ti6Al4V, Bałasz et al. (2023) reported two UA batches with count-based PSD values of D10/D50/D90 = 40.2/52.0/60.8 and 41.2/51.4/63.4 µm, and span values of 0.37 and 0.43, respectively (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10). The D50 values differed by ~1 µm, suggesting modest batch-to-batch variation, but with n = 2 and different underlying conditions, no statistical conclusion can be drawn.

For niobium, Wróbel et al. (2026) reported a single-batch PSD of D10/D50/D90 = 44.12/54.99/66.85 µm and span = 0.413 (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12). No replicate data exist.

---

## (b) Spread in Yield

**No study reports replicate-run yield statistics (SD or CV) at fixed settings.** The available yield data vary considerably across alloys and equipment configurations, but always reflect parameter studies rather than replicate production runs:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** 45–50 wt.% of input rods converted to particles <100 µm, reported as a pooled range across three batches without batch-specific values (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).
- **AlSi12 (Yankin 2025):** Approximately 75% of the total powder passed a 63 µm sieve and was considered suitable for SLM (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Usable-powder yield ranged from 47% to 63% across the 18 process conditions. The highest yield (63%) was at minimum current (70 A) and lowest amplitude (60%). At amplitude-grouped averages: 59% at 60%, 53% at 70%, and 51% at 80% amplitude (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** 94% of feed wire converted to powder <100 µm; 70.3% by mass in the 43–83 µm (63 ± 20 µm) range; after gas-flow optimization, >98% recovery was claimed (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10).
- **Recycled Ti alloy (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder):** Over 85% of atomized powder was below 100 µm (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6).

The yield variation across process conditions for 316L (47–63%, a range of 16 percentage points) provides the closest proxy for the sensitivity of yield to process perturbations (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

---

## (c) Spread in Sphericity, Circularity, Aspect Ratio, and Satellite Fraction

**No published study reports run-to-run variability (SD or CV) for sphericity or satellite fraction.** The available data are:

- **Mo–Si–Ti (Hinrichs 2021):** Greater than 90% of particles had aspect ratio <1.2 across all three batches, with particles described as satellite-free (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). No batch-specific sphericity distributions were tabulated.
- **Nb (Wróbel 2026):** Mean sphericity 0.94; satellites, agglomerates, and oxidation defects were not observed (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12).
- **316L recycled (Bashmakova 2026):** Sphericity coefficient ranged from 0.84 to 0.90 across 18 process conditions, compared with 0.56 for virgin gas-atomized powder (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 7-9). The range of 0.06 across conditions is a proxy for process-induced shape variability.
- **Ti6Al4V (Bałasz et al. 2023):** Mean sphericity 0.88–0.90 for the two reported UA entries (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 8-10).
- **Sn–58Bi (Yang et al. 2026):** At the optimized condition (30% amplitude, 199 °C, Ar), sphericity = 0.87 and satellite index = 1.07. Sphericity decreased and satellite index increased with melt temperature (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15).

---

## (d) Run-to-Run Variation in Composition and Oxygen Pickup

**The Hinrichs et al. (2021) Mo–Si–Ti dataset is the only published study with batch-specific oxygen measurements at fixed nominal UA settings.** The three batches yielded: S1 = 1450 ± 20 wt.ppm O, S2 = 1330 ± 10 wt.ppm O, S3 = 1280 ± 30 wt.ppm O (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7). Starting from a common as-cast oxygen content of ~460 ppm, the oxygen pickup during atomization was approximately 820–990 ppm per batch. The inter-batch mean is ~1353 ppm, with a batch-to-batch sample standard deviation of approximately 87 ppm and coefficient of variation of approximately 6.4%. ICP-OES analysis showed no significant changes in alloy composition (Mo, Si, Ti) across the three batches (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 7-9, hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).

For **316L stainless steel** (Bashmakova et al. 2026), the main alloying elements (Cr, Ni, Mo) remained within specification across the two extreme atomization conditions (70A/60% vs. 160A/80%). The most notable compositional change was a three-fold reduction in manganese content (from 0.88 wt.% in virgin powder to 0.27–0.28 wt.% in both atomized samples), attributed primarily to Mn evaporation during PBF-LB and atomization (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 11-13). Oxygen content was consistently elevated relative to the virgin powder, with higher current yielding higher oxygen and larger vibration amplitude tending to reduce it; nitrogen remained nearly unchanged (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

For **recycled Ti alloy** (Ciftci et al. 2025, AMAZEMET rePowder), the oxygen pickup during UA from machining chips was approximately 220 ppm, with total powder oxygen below 600 ppm, meeting ASTM F2924 requirements (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6).

---

## Absence of True Replicate Data for Aluminum Alloys

**No published study was found reporting true replicate-run (fixed-setting, batch-to-batch) UA data for any aluminum alloy** — including AlSi10Mg, AlSi12, 6061, 6063, or Scalmalloy. The Yankin et al. (2025) AlSi12 study comes closest by reporting PSD across multiple process conditions on a 3D Lab ATO system, but each condition was run once, and measurement-level uncertainty was not published (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). The same gap exists for copper (only single-batch characterizations exist for UA of recycled copper), magnesium alloys, nickel-based superalloys, and high-entropy alloys processed by sonotrode UA.

---

## Closest Proxies: Parameter-Sensitivity Ranges

In the absence of true replicate data, the ranges observed across deliberate parameter changes provide upper bounds on expected run-to-run variability if those parameters are well-controlled. The following table summarizes the dominant sources of variability identified in the literature:

| Process variable | Reported effect on PSD | Reported effect on yield | Reported effect on morphology | Reported effect on chemistry / oxygen | Key reference(s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ultrasonic frequency (typically 35–60 kHz) | Primary theoretical control of capillary wavelength and droplet diameter; doubling frequency is predicted to reduce particle size by approximately 40%. | Higher frequency can increase atomization throughput, but fixed-setting comparative yield data are unavailable. | Finer droplets generally solidify faster, potentially limiting deformation and collisions; no replicate shape statistics reported. | Indirect effect through droplet size, surface area and cooling rate; quantitative oxygen dependence not reported. | Bałasz et al. (2023) (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5); Hinrichs et al. (2021) (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 9-11) |
| Vibration amplitude | Higher amplitude strengthens capillary waves and cavitation and generally produces finer droplets. In AlSi12 it was the third-ranked powder-quality factor; in Sn–58Bi, span was 1.909 at 30% versus 2.079 at 20%. Transitional behavior can cause local PSD fluctuations. | For recycled 316L, mean usable yield declined from 59% at 60% amplitude to 53% at 70% and 51% at 80%, although interactions with current were present. | Higher amplitude increased Sn–58Bi sphericity and reduced its satellite index; the optimized condition gave sphericity 0.87 and satellite index 1.07. | Larger amplitude tended to reduce 316L oxygen, attributed to shorter liquid–atmosphere interaction time; no fixed-setting replicate statistic was reported. | Yankin et al. (2025) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11); Yang et al. (2026) (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10) |
| Electrical current / arc power | Ranked the strongest experimental factor for AlSi12: increasing current from 140 to 150 A significantly reduced D10 and D50 and increased span. Current controls melting rate, superheat and melt fluidity; excessive values can destabilize the arc. | In 316L, yield varied with current and amplitude; higher current generally favored yield within the stable window, but both under-melting and excessive arc intensity reduced process stability. | Changes droplet formation and breakup stability through melt viscosity and delivery rate; no independent fixed-setting shape spread reported. | Higher current raised 316L oxygen, consistent with higher melt temperature and stronger high-temperature oxidation. Main alloying elements were comparatively insensitive over the tested range. | Yankin et al. (2025) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2); Bashmakova et al. (2026) (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11) |
| Arc/torch angle or position | Second-ranked AlSi12 factor. Powder suitability varied nonlinearly with torch angle and worsened sharply above 0°; changing angle altered D10 and, to a lesser extent, D50 and D90. | No numerical angle-specific conversion yield was published. | Changes where and how the molten drop contacts the vibrating surface, affecting film formation and breakup; quantitative shape spread was not reported. | No angle-specific composition or oxygen data were reported. | Yankin et al. (2025) (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2) |
| Melt superheat / temperature | Competing effects: decreasing viscosity and surface tension initially promotes film spreading and finer droplets, whereas oxidation, coalescence and incomplete spheroidization at excessive temperature can coarsen and broaden the PSD. Sn–58Bi D50 reached a minimum of 91.6 µm at 259 °C and increased to 106.3 µm at 499 °C. | A sufficiently superheated, low-viscosity melt is necessary for stable atomization; no replicated temperature-specific yields were reported. | For Sn–58Bi, increasing temperature reduced sphericity and increased satellites because lower surface tension weakened spheroidization and prolonged liquid lifetime. | Sn–58Bi oxygen first decreased and then increased with temperature, with a minimum near 259 °C; high temperature promoted oxide-film formation. Volatile-element evaporation is also a risk. | Yang et al. (2026) (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15); Hinrichs et al. (2021) (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 9-11); Ciftci et al. (2025) (ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 1-3, ciftcli2025alloydevelopmentfrom pages 3-6) |
| Wire-feed or melt-flow rate | Melt delivery must match the arc’s melting capacity and the plate’s atomization capacity. Excess flow can accumulate molten metal on the sonotrode and move breakup outside the stable capillary-wave regime. | Five of 16 planned 316L runs were interrupted/excluded because of instability associated particularly with excessive feed or insufficient current. | Unstable feed produces irregular breakup and greater morphology variation; retained runs were mostly spherical, but no run-level sphericity SD was given. | Longer residence or excess molten inventory may increase oxidation or evaporation, but the cited study did not quantify oxygen by feed rate. | Bałasz et al. (2024) (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4) |

Argon reduced the Sn–58Bi contact angle relative to air. | Chemical interaction, erosion or dissolution of sonotrode material can contaminate powder; quantitative batch-to-batch contamination data remain sparse. | Yang et al. (2026) (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15); Szostak-Staropiętka et al. (2025) (scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5) |

Key quantitative proxies include:

- **AlSi12 parameter study (Yankin 2025):** Span (the most sensitive PSD metric) varied by 37.5% across three process variables, while D50 varied by only 4.4% (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2).
- **316L parameter study (Bashmakova 2026):** D50 ranged from 23 to 34 µm (a factor of ~1.5×) and yield from 47% to 63% across 18 conditions; 70% vibration amplitude conditions showed anomalous PSD fluctuations attributed to transitional capillary-wave breakup (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 9-11).
- **Sn–58Bi temperature study (Yang 2026):** D50 ranged from 91.6 to 106.3 µm (16% variation) across a 300 °C superheat range, with competing effects of viscosity reduction and oxidation (yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15).
- **Process stability failures (Bałasz 2024, 316L):** 5 of 16 planned atomization runs were excluded due to process instability, predominantly at high wire-feed speeds or low currents, illustrating the sharp boundaries of the stable operating window (bałasz2024aninvestigationof pages 2-4).

---

## Summary and Conclusions

1. **True batch-to-batch replicate data are essentially absent** for UA of molten metals. Only Hinrichs et al. (2021) provide a three-batch comparison for Mo–Si–Ti, finding d90 values of 63–78 µm, consistent >85% yield in the 40–80 µm range, aspect ratios <1.2 for >90% of particles, and oxygen contents of 1280–1450 ppm with a batch-to-batch CV of ~6.4% (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7).

2. **For aluminum alloys, no replicate-run statistics exist** in the published literature through mid-2026. PSD and yield data are available for AlSi12 but only as single-run parameter studies (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 2-3).

3. **Parameter-sensitivity studies provide proxy bounds:** At fixed frequency, D50 appears relatively stable (CV < 5% for AlSi12 across parameter changes), while the distribution span and the fine-particle fraction (D10) are more sensitive (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4). Yield varies by ~16 percentage points across current/amplitude settings for 316L (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15).

4. **Sphericity and satellite metrics** are reported condition-by-condition but never with replicate-based uncertainty. Values of 0.84–0.94 for sphericity and satellite-free to satellite-index 1.07 are typical for optimized UA conditions across alloys (wrobel2026enhancingniobiumpowder pages 10-12, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 7-9, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 5-10).

5. **Oxygen pickup** is a systematic concern. The one three-batch oxygen dataset shows ~6.4% CV (hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 4-7); alloy composition was stable across batches for Mo-Si-Ti and across process conditions for 316L (bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 11-13, hinrichs2021flexiblepowderproduction pages 7-9).

6. **The dominant process variables** identified as sources of powder variability are, in approximate order of influence: ultrasonic frequency (theoretical), electrical current/arc power (strongest experimentally observed), arc/torch angle, vibration amplitude, melt superheat/temperature, wire-feed rate, atmosphere purity, sonotrode wetting, and chamber gas-flow pattern (yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 3-4, bashmakova2026ontheultrasonic pages 13-15, yang2026effectsofultrasonic pages 10-15, yankin2025effectofultrasonic pages 1-2, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 7-8, scientific2023comparisonofultrasonic pages 4-5).

This review confirms a significant gap in the published UA literature: the absence of formal repeatability studies following standard metrological practice (replicate production runs, reported SD/CV, documented number of replicates) for any alloy system, and particularly for the aluminum alloys of greatest interest for additive manufacturing.

info.query: For ultrasonic atomization of molten metals (sonotrode or vibrating-plate ultrasonic atomization, e.g. AMAZEMET rePowder, 3D Lab ATO Lab / ATO One, or lab-built 20-60 kHz systems), what published data exist on run-to-run or batch-to-batch repeatability at fixed process settings? Report, with numbers and citations: (a) the spread in particle size distribution (D10/D50/D90, span, or mass fraction in 15-45 um or 20-63 um) across replicate runs (standard deviation or coefficient of variation, and the number of replicates); (b) the spread in yield (fraction of the charge converted to powder, and fraction in the target size cut); (c) the spread in sphericity, circularity, aspect ratio or satellite fraction; (d) run-to-run variation in composition or oxygen pickup. Prioritize aluminum alloys (AlSi10Mg, Al-Si, 6xxx such as 6061/6063, Scalmalloy) but include other alloys (Ti, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mg, refractory). If true replicate data are absent, say so explicitly and give the closest proxies (error bars in parameter studies of amplitude, frequency or melt feed rate; repeated-measurement scatter), and list the process variables the literature identifies as the dominant sources of variability (amplitude, frequency, melt superheat, melt flow rate, sonotrode/plate material and temperature, wetting, oxygen).
